title: A supervisor fault during suspend kills the process on the SystemEvents thread
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E6, on exactly the code path the implementer flagged as the piece it was least sure about. Good instinct.

SystemEventSupervisorAdapter.OnSuspend calls WaitForSuspendDrainAsync().GetAwaiter().GetResult(), and WaitForSuspendDrainAsync deliberately awaits the supervisor task 'to observe/rethrow any fault'. In production that rethrow lands on Microsoft.Win32.SystemEvents' dedicated notification thread, inside Win32SystemEventSource.OnPowerModeChanged, with no catch above it. Unhandled exception on a non-main thread terminates the process.

The sibling handlers (OnResume, OnNetworkAddressChanged) route through FireAndForget and log. Suspend is the ONLY one that propagates.

IT IS REACHABLE, not theoretical. MountSupervisor.EnqueueAndWait catches EVERY exception from the queued action and re-surfaces it via completion.TrySetException, so any unexpected throw during the drain sweep - an invalid-transition guard, a collection mutated during iteration, a missing host config - arrives as a faulted task rather than a log line.

AND THE CONSEQUENCE COMPOUNDS. A process that dies during suspend never runs any resume-side handling. The mounts are left exactly as the machine went to sleep with them, which is the wedged-drive-on-wake scenario the whole project exists to prevent - reached by the handler that was supposed to prevent it.

FIX: catch and log in the suspend handler like its siblings do. The fault must not escape onto the OS notification thread. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 should also say what the suspend handler does with a supervisor fault, since it currently says nothing (see the spec-gaps issue).

Everything else about the blocking wrapper survived the attack: the Task.WhenAny-against-a-budget race is genuinely bounded, it does return, and it does not cancel the in-flight drain.

title: Resume ignores hosts that slept while Mounted, and never reconciles against listmounts
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E6. This is the maintainer's number one real-world scenario.

MountSupervisor.ResumeAsync switches on state and handles Disabled, Ready and Unreachable. Mounted and Mounting fall into default:, commented 'Mounting/Mounted should not exist here (suspend already drained them)'.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6 says the opposite in as many words:
  'Machine sleeps with mounts up | Unmount on suspend. IF WE MISSED IT, FORCE-UNMOUNT AND RECONCILE ON RESUME.'
And §3 from the other side: 'accept that a forced unmount may be needed on resume'. §3's event table maps Resume to 'Re-probe ALL immediately'.

The assumption is only safe if suspend ALWAYS succeeds. It is best-effort by design: bounded by a budget that can elapse (that is what E6's WhenAny race exists for), and now also defeated outright by the fault-kills-the-process bug. So the case the code assumes cannot happen is the case that happens.

Worse, resume never calls mount/listmounts AT ALL. The state surviving a suspend is the least trustworthy state the app ever holds - rclone's child process, WinFsp and the network stack have all been through a power transition - and it is the only moment where nothing re-derives ground truth. The 30-second periodic reconciliation is a cadence, not the resume-time guarantee §6 asks for.

FIX: on resume, force-probe hosts that are still Mounted, and reconcile intended state against mount/listmounts before trusting anything.

RELATED, and the deeper reason this slipped through: §3's event table gives NETWORK CHANGE the stronger treatment ('re-probe all immediately; force-probe mounted hosts') and RESUME only 're-probe all immediately'. The implementation read that asymmetry as 'resume touches no mounted host'. Resume is more likely to need it than a network change, not less. One of those two rows is wrong - see the spec-gaps issue.

title: A dead mount on a LIVE host is undetectable — the mounted probe is TCP-only
description:
Found by re-examining the design against the maintainer's ACTUAL hardware and failure modes, after establishing that the laptop dock/undock scenario the spec is built around does not apply to him (desktop + Mac laptop; Bosun is Windows-only).

While a host is Mounted, the recurring check is HandleMountedProbeDueAsync -> ProbeShallowAsync(hostname, port). That is a TCP connect to the NAS on port 22. It never touches the mount.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 already states the principle - "TCP success does not imply SFTP success. Never mount on a shallow probe alone" - but applies it only to the transition INTO Mounting. Once mounted, the deep probe never runs again. ADR-011 made mounted hosts ALWAYS probed; it did not change WHAT the probe checks.

THE FAILURE, and it is the maintainer's two most likely scenarios rather than an edge case:

  1. OVERNIGHT SLEEP. Desktop sleeps with a mount up. The NAS stays on the same LAN and keeps answering port 22, but the SSH channel under the mount dies - timed out, sshd restarted, session reaped. On wake the shallow probe SUCCEEDS, ConsecutiveMountedFailures resets to zero, the supervisor believes all is well, and every filesystem call into that drive hangs. Explorer freezes.

  2. NETWORK INTERRUPTION. A blip shorter than failures_before_unmount x interval never trips the unmount, but is easily long enough to kill the SSH channel. Host returns, probe passes, mount is dead. Identical signature.

In both cases nothing unmounts it, because by the only measure Bosun takes the host is healthy. This is an Invariant I2 hole that ADR-005's whole design misses, because ADR-005 assumes the host becoming UNREACHABLE is what signals trouble.

I8 (unmount on suspend) defends case 1 IF the drain completes - but §3 says it is best-effort and a forced unmount may still be needed on resume, and bs-ajh showed the suspend budget was unreachable until recently. I8 does not defend case 2 at all.

RECOMMENDED FIX: a periodic DEEP probe for mounted hosts, at a lower cadence than the shallow probe, with its own documented interval (say global.mounted_deep_probe_interval_seconds). operations/list goes to rclone rcd over loopback HTTP, so it is bounded by the HttpClient timeout and does NOT touch the wedged filesystem path.

DO NOT probe the mount by enumerating the drive letter directly. That is precisely the call that hangs, and the supervisor's channel is GLOBALLY serialised (see MountSupervisor class remarks) - one hung enumeration would stall every other host, converting a one-drive wedge into a total supervisor stall. If that is ever wanted it must be strictly out-of-band with a hard timeout.

This is an amendment to ADR-011 in substance: that ADR settled that mounted hosts are always probed, and this settles what the probe has to be to mean anything. Per the validation-audit principle, any new interval needs a documented range and validation.
close_reason: Periodic mounted deep probe added with its own interval, counter and threshold; a shallow-passing/deep-failing host now reaches Draining. Mutation-verified. ADR-016 records the design and the rejected shared-counter approach

title: rcd rejects every endpoint but core/version with 403 — Bosun cannot mount, probe, or provision against real rclone
description:
Found by verifying rc endpoints against the REAL rclone v1.75.0, and confirmed independently by the orchestrator. This is the highest-impact defect found so far, and no unit test could have caught it.

EVERY rc endpoint except core/version returns 403 unless rcd is started with --rc-no-auth or real credentials:

  {"error":"authentication must be set up on the rc server to use \"config/create\" or the --rc-no-auth flag must be in use"}

Confirmed for config/create, config/get, mount/listmounts and operations/list. So against a real rclone TODAY, RcloneProcessService can call core/version and nothing else: remote provisioning, mounting, unmounting, reconciliation and the deep probe would all 403.

That is the entire application. It also explains why nothing caught it: core/version is the only endpoint the existing integration test exercises, and every other test fakes IRcloneClient.

THE CITATION IN THE CODE IS WRONG. RcloneProcessService.BuildStartInfo's remarks state that a loopback bind needs no --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-no-auth, citing rclone.org's rcd page. That is not rclone v1.75.0's behaviour. CLAUDE.md names rc parameter names as one of two areas where secondhand information is routinely wrong; this is that, one level up - the auth model rather than a parameter name.

RECOMMENDED FIX, verified empirically by the orchestrator rather than proposed from documentation:

Generate a cryptographically random per-launch credential, pass it to the child via the RCLONE_RC_USER and RCLONE_RC_PASS ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, and have RcloneClient's HttpClient send Basic auth. Verified working against v1.75.0:

  correct Basic auth  -> 200 {"mountPoints": []}
  no auth             -> 401 Unauthorized
  wrong password      -> 401 Unauthorized

WHY ENV VARS RATHER THAN --rc-user/--rc-pass ON THE COMMAND LINE: a command line is readable by any process running as the same user via Win32_Process.CommandLine. We know this precisely because Bosun's own ISessionMonitor does exactly that to enumerate ssh.exe. Putting the rc password there would hand it to anything that looks. Environment variables are not perfect either, but they are not trivially enumerable the same way.

WHY NOT --rc-no-auth: it disables auth for ALL local callers. rcd is loopback-only, so the exposure is other processes running as this user - which is a lower bar than it sounds, and the whole point of the rc API is that it can mount and unmount filesystems. A random per-launch secret costs about fifteen lines and removes that surface entirely. There is no ergonomic cost: the secret is generated, used, and discarded within one process lifetime, and never persisted.

Secondary consideration for whoever implements it: rclone also supports --rc-htpasswd. Not obviously better here, since it means writing a credential file to disk.

BLOCKS the v1 definition of done items 2 through 5 - everything involving a mount. Does NOT block item 1 (Terminal profiles), which needs no rclone at all.
close_reason: Fixed: random 32-byte per-lifetime credential via RCLONE_RC_USER/PASS env vars, Basic auth on every request. Verified against real rclone v1.75.0; log-leak guard mutation-tested

title: WinFsp absent does not disable mounting — hosts retry mount/mount forever
description:
Found during validation of E12b, and flagged honestly by the implementer.

ADR-012 and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6 both say WinFsp absent means MOUNT FEATURES ARE DISABLED while terminal features keep working. That is not what happens. WinFsp detection currently feeds StartupReadiness and nothing else - nothing gates MountSupervisor.

So with WinFsp missing, a persistent host will:
  1. pass its shallow probe (TCP)
  2. PASS ITS DEEP PROBE - operations/list works fine over SFTP and needs no WinFsp at all
  3. call mount/mount, which fails
  4. drain, back off, and retry FOREVER on the DrainCause.MountFailure ladder

against something that cannot possibly succeed until the user installs software. The only signal is a StartupReadiness field that nothing renders yet.

WHY THIS IS P0 RATHER THAN COSMETIC: WinFsp is NOT installed on the maintainer's machine (bs-z8u), so this is the exact path a first run takes today. It also quietly reintroduces the shape of bs-k4k - an unbounded retry against a permanent failure - now paced by backoff rather than spinning, but still endless, still noisy in the target server's auth log, and still with no distinct reason surfaced at the layer where it happens.

FIX DIRECTION: the supervisor needs a mounting-availability gate. Hosts should still probe (shallow probing needs neither WinFsp nor rclone, and live reachability in the tray is genuinely useful) but must never enter Mounting while mounting is unavailable, and the per-host reason must be visible in the snapshot. That is literally ADR-012 Decision 3's worked example - 'P: is not mounted - WinFsp is not installed' - so the string the tray needs is already specified.

Note this generalises beyond WinFsp: rclone rcd being down is the same condition. One gate, several causes.

The implementer declined to add the coupling unprompted and flagged it instead, which was the right call - this is a spec-vs-implementation gap, not an implementation detail.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: E12b — Startup orchestrator: the ordered sequence
description:
One hosted service owning the ordered sequence from ADR-012 Decision 1:

    load config -> detect WinFsp -> start rclone rcd + health check
      -> provision remotes -> adopt-or-clear existing mounts -> run the supervisor

The order is load-bearing, not stylistic:
  - Remotes must exist before any deep probe can pass. I1 forbids mounting without a passing deep probe, and the probe targets a remote that config/create has to have written first. This is the bs-bw4 gap.
  - Adopt-or-clear must precede the supervisor loop. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6 requires surviving mounts to be reconciled 'before doing anything else', because a mount left from a crashed run is the drive letter most likely pointing somewhere wrong - and after bs-ka9, adoption is Fs-aware, so this is where a wrong-host mount gets cleared rather than adopted.

Each step reports success/failure into a typed readiness value rather than throwing. A step failing disables what depends on it and leaves everything else running.

Also resolves bs-127: register RcloneProcessService as a hosted service. Per ADR-012, the lazy-config pattern it was avoiding is a TEST concern that leaked into production design - tests build a host WITHOUT the orchestrator registered. Fix the test, not the architecture.

Acceptance: one test per failure mode - no config, invalid config, no WinFsp, no rclone binary, rcd fails to start, provisioning fails for one host but not others. Each asserts what is disabled AND what still works.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: E12a — Pre-logger failure reporting (bs-16b, blocker for the rest)
description:
ADR-012's catastrophic path shows a MessageBox and exits. That path exists precisely because nothing else is available yet - no tray icon, and per bs-16b no logger either.

Today App.OnStartup registers the unhandled-exception handlers, then builds the host, THEN resolves ILogger<App>. Both handlers log via `_logger?.` - a null-conditional. So any exception before the logger resolves is swallowed entirely: no file, no debug sink, no dialog. CreateHost() can genuinely throw - it calls Directory.CreateDirectory on %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs, which fails on a permissions problem, a redirected roaming profile, or a full disk. ADR-010 explicitly courts users on domain-joined machines where redirected AppData is common.

DO THIS FIRST. Every other part of ADR-012 assumes something reaches the user.

- A minimal bootstrap diagnostic channel installed BEFORE CreateHost() is called, which itself cannot throw
- The catastrophic presentation (MessageBox naming the reason, then exit) behind an INJECTABLE interface so no test ever pops a dialog
- Windows Event Log or a fixed fallback file are both reasonable durable sinks; pick one and say why

Acceptance: a test forces CreateHost() to throw (unwritable log directory) and asserts the failure is both reported through the injected notifier and durably recorded. No test displays a real dialog.
close_reason: Bootstrap diagnostics delivered and validated: 345/345, dual durable sink, catastrophic notifier behind an injectable seam, terminal pre-logger gap closed and mutation-verified

title: E12 — Startup contract (ADR-012)
description:
Implements ADR-012, ratified 2026-08-16. Not in the original docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md - this epic exists because five epics each correctly deferred a question none of them owned, and the deferrals accumulated into a gap that currently stops the tool working at all.

Subsumes bs-bw4 (provisioner wired nowhere), bs-127 (hosted service / ordering), bs-o09 (config location), and depends on bs-16b (pre-logger failures reach nobody).

Read ADR-012 in full before starting. The presentation table is the spec for what the user sees.
close_reason: E12 startup contract complete: ordered sequence, fail-soft readiness, mounting-availability gate, config at %LOCALAPPDATA% with first-run bootstrap

title: Ratify or amend ADR-012 — the startup contract
description: ADR-012 is PROPOSED in docs/DECISIONS.md and nothing has been implemented against it. It answers, as one contract: the ordered startup sequence, fail-soft degradation for every step, invalid-config behaviour, typed readiness for the tray, and where hosts.toml lives. Resolves bs-bw4, bs-127, bs-o09 and raises the urgency of bs-16b. Ratify, amend, or reject - implementation of bs-bw4 is blocked on this.
notes: ADR-012 REWRITTEN after the maintainer objected that fail-soft leaves the user to notice nothing is working. The objection was correct and the original draft conflated fail-fast with fail-silent. Now: four conditions, four channels (MessageBox+exit for catastrophic, persistent error icon + toast for missing dependency, immediate toast for invalid config, first-run WINDOW for no config). Adds a hard requirement that the tray icon encodes aggregate health at a glance, and promotes bs-16b to a blocker.
close_reason: ADR-012 ratified by the maintainer 2026-08-16; status flipped to Accepted

title: Flaky: RcloneProcessServiceTests.LaunchFailed_retries_after_RestartDelay_and_can_then_become_Healthy
description:
Observed ONCE by the independent test author during a mutation run, and not reproduced across eight subsequent runs (five clean, three mutated). Outside the supervisor, and unrelated to anything that agent touched.

Worth chasing rather than writing off, for one reason: it is in the component that owns rclone rcd's LIFETIME. If RcloneProcessService's restart path has a genuine race, the production symptom is not a red test - it is rcd failing to come back after a crash, which means every mount silently stops working and the supervisor's reconciliation has nothing to talk to.

Related known hazard, already fixed once in this area: E3 found that Task.WaitAsync(CancellationToken) does not guarantee its continuation runs inline on the completing thread, which breaks the synchronous-continuation determinism the FakeTimeProvider testing style depends on. That fix removed WaitAsync from StopAsync. A similar cross-thread dependency may remain in the restart path.

If it cannot be reproduced, say so plainly and leave this open rather than closing it as unreproducible - an intermittent failure that disappears when you look at it is exactly the kind that returns under CI load on a slower machine.
notes:
REPRODUCED AND DIAGNOSED (2026-08-16), by the agent fixing the E5 defects.

Reproduction rate: ~1 in 50-100. Seen twice across roughly 280 isolated runs of the test and ~70
full-suite runs. So it is real, not an observer artefact.

MECHANISM (diagnosed from source; assertion text not captured because the failure window is too
narrow to log reliably):

RcloneProcessService.SuperviseAsync runs as a detached background Task driven by
Task.Delay(options.RestartDelay, timeProvider, cancellationToken). Unlike the supervisor's
channel-based tests or HostProbe's, THAT Task.Delay overload's continuation is not guaranteed to
resume synchronously/inline when FakeTimeProvider.Advance() fires the underlying timer - it can hop
to a ThreadPool thread.

The test's PumpAsync() helper (64x Task.Yield()) is a best-effort, non-deterministic wait for that
hop to complete before asserting launcher.StartCalls.Count == 2. Under load the hop sometimes does
not complete in time.

This is the SAME CLASS of race that E3 already found and hardened against at a different call site:
Task.WaitAsync(CancellationToken) in StopAsync, fixed by removing WaitAsync and documented in a
comment in that file. AdvanceUntilCompleteAsync was written for that case;
LaunchFailed_retries_after_RestartDelay_and_can_then_become_Healthy never got the same treatment.

Deliberately NOT fixed as part of the E5 defect pass - out of scope, and the real fix (make
RcloneProcessService's Task.Delay usage resume deterministically under FakeTimeProvider, mirroring
AdvanceUntilCompleteAsync) deserves its own targeted change and review.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS BEYOND THE TEST: if the underlying resumption assumption is wrong in the
PRODUCTION path rather than only in the test harness, the symptom is rcd failing to come back after
a crash - every mount silently stops working, and the supervisor reconciles against nothing. Worth
confirming which of the two it is before dismissing this as test-only flakiness.
FIRED ON CI 2026-08-16, blocking the integration PR (#10, run 31949918538). Exactly the scenario predicted in the earlier note: an intermittent failure that disappears when you look at it returns under CI load on a slower machine. Locally it reproduces at roughly 1 in 50-100; a GitHub runner is slower and more contended, so the odds are worse there. Promoted to P0 - it is no longer a curiosity, it is a merge blocker and it will keep randomly reddening unrelated PRs until fixed.
FIXED. Reproduced on the FIRST isolated run with the actual assertion captured: "Assert.Equal() Failure: Expected: Healthy, Actual: Starting" - launcher.StartCalls.Count == 2 had already passed, so the second AttemptStartAsync had started but had not yet reached SetStatus(Healthy) when the assertion ran.

VERDICT: TEST-HARNESS DEFECT, NOT PRODUCTION. Evidence: FakeRcloneClient.GetVersionAsync returns an already-completed task, so once the continuation resumes at all, everything from launcher.Start() through SetStatus(Healthy) runs synchronously - there is no second race point downstream. The only gap is the resumption of Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider, CancellationToken) itself, whose continuation the BCL may queue to the ThreadPool rather than resume inline. PumpAsync (64x Task.Yield) was a bet on the pool scheduling that queued work item in time, and loses under a cold pool - which is what an isolated dotnet test process looks like at startup, and what a CI runner looks like generally.

Production is unaffected: SuperviseAsync is a detached background loop, nothing awaits its continuation synchronously from elsewhere, and a real TimeProvider.System timer always fires on a ThreadPool thread anyway - the hop this test exposed is the NORMAL behaviour of a real timer, not a new hazard. StatusChanged subscribers already have to tolerate arbitrary-thread invocation. RcloneProcessService.cs was correctly left untouched.

FIX: replaced the two fixed-yield-count waits with AdvanceAndWaitUntilAsync, which polls the actual asserted condition on a bounded real-time budget, mirroring the AdvanceUntilCompleteAsync pattern already in the file for the same hazard. Assertions unchanged - only how long the test waits before failing on its own. No retry attributes, no Thread.Sleep tolerance, no skips.

ALSO FIXED, latent: An_unexpected_exit_while_Healthy_triggers_restart_and_reconciliation_signal had the identical shape (advance time to trigger a restart Task.Delay, then assert Healthy) and was flaky by the same mechanism - it simply had not rolled a bad enough die yet. Recorded here so a future reader diffing only the reported test name does not think it was untouched.

A sweep found no other test using the pattern: the probe tests await the production Task directly (race-free regardless of completing thread), and the config-store retention tests have no async gap at all.

VERIFIED: agent ran 120/120 isolated, 60/60 on the latent test, 100/100 full suite. Orchestrator independently ran 25/25 full suite. Build warning-clean.
close_reason: Test-harness race fixed at both affected sites; 125 independent full-suite runs green; production code correctly untouched

title: RATIFY spec amendment: rate-limit the failed-mount cycle (bug fixed in PR #8)
description:
Found by INDEPENDENT adversarial testing of E5. The most serious defect found so far.

A PERSISTENT host whose deep probe fails while TCP still answers - an expired key, the SFTP subsystem disabled, an ordinary real-world case - spins:

    Ready -> Mounting -> Draining -> Disabled -> Probing -> Ready -> ...

with NO CLOCK ADVANCE ANYWHERE IN THE CYCLE. CompleteDrainAsync auto-re-enables, EnableHostAsync shallow-probes (succeeds, because TCP is fine), OnEnteredReadyAsync auto-mounts, the deep probe fails again.

The loop is STACK-RECURSIVE:
    OnEnteredReadyAsync -> TryBeginMountAsync -> BeginDrainAsync -> AttemptDrainStepAsync -> CompleteDrainAsync -> EnableHostAsync -> ...

In production it pegs a core, floods the target server's auth log and rclone with operations/list and mount/unmount as fast as the network allows, and terminates in a StackOverflowException, which .NET does not allow any catch block to intercept - the process dies. Bosun dying is itself an I2 hazard: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6 handles a crash-with-mounts-up via adopt-or-clear on next start, but only if the user restarts it.

The adversarial test's fake caps failures at 25 so the test reports a number instead of hanging. Production has no such cap.

The same loop occurs via a permanently failing mount/mount - which is precisely §6's 'drive letter already in use' row, where the REQUIRED behaviour is 'refuse the mount, surface the conflict in the tray, do not silently pick another letter'. Retrying forever is the opposite.

WHY THE ORIGINAL SUITE MISSED IT: the implementer's own test for deep-probe failure uses an ON-DEMAND host, which does not auto-mount, so the loop breaks after one pass. Its mount-failure test uses a fake whose failure is consumed on first use. Both are reasonable-looking tests that happen to avoid the cycle.

ROOT CAUSE IS A SPEC GAP: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 draws this cycle and never rate-limits it. §4's Backoff section paces Unreachable -> Probing but says nothing about a host that is reachable and simply cannot be mounted.

SPEC AMENDMENT NEEDED: §4 requires an explicit rule for a failed MOUNT ATTEMPT, distinct from a failed probe. Repeated mount failure against a reachable host must be paced, and probably surfaced - a host that answers TCP but cannot be mounted is a condition the user needs to see, not one to retry silently forever.

A fix is in progress routing mount-failure drains through backoff pacing and breaking the recursion. This issue tracks ratifying the resulting spec amendment.
notes: CODE FIX LANDED in PR #8 and is mutation-verified. What remains is ratifying the spec: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 Backoff still only covers Unreachable -> Probing and says nothing about a reachable host that cannot be mounted. The implementation now paces every mount-attempt failure through its own backoff ladder. Confirm that shape, or choose "N free retries then pace" instead.

title: Startup adoption matches drive letter only — can adopt another host's live mount
description:
Found by INDEPENDENT adversarial testing of E5.

AdoptOrClearExistingMountsAsync matches surviving mounts on DRIVE LETTER ONLY, ignoring the Fs the mount actually serves.

Scenario, made of two entirely ordinary events:
  1. A previous run mounted P: serving bosun-previous-owner:/somewhere/else.
  2. The user edits hosts.toml and assigns P: to a different host, prod.
  3. Bosun starts, sees a mount at P:, and ADOPTS it as prod's mount.

Result: the supervisor reports prod as Mounted at P:. Nothing hangs. Nothing is logged as wrong. The user opens P:, sees files, and reads and writes on a server they did not choose.

This is worse than a wedge in one specific way: a wedged drive is obvious and self-announcing, whereas this fails silently and the failure mode is WRITING DATA TO THE WRONG HOST. For a tool whose users run production boxes and bastion hosts, that is the more expensive error.

Drive-letter reassignment is ordinary config editing, and a surviving mount is exactly what §6's crash-recovery row is about ('On next start, enumerate existing mounts via mount/listmounts and adopt or clear them before doing anything else'). The two coincide easily - edit the config, restart Bosun after a crash.

mount/listmounts returns Fs alongside MountPoint and E3 already models it, so the information needed is present and simply unused.

FIX: adopt only when BOTH the mount point AND the Fs match what that host would mount. Otherwise clear and mount fresh. Fix in progress.

The spec should also say this explicitly: §6's crash-recovery row says 'adopt or clear them' without stating what makes a mount adoptable, which is how the gap arose.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8: adoption now requires Fs to match, mismatches cleared and remounted; mutation-verified

title: IRcloneRemoteProvisioner is wired nowhere — no remote exists, so every mount fails
description:
Found by the E5 implementer while building the supervisor, and confirmed by grep: IRcloneRemoteProvisioner is referenced ONLY by its own interface and implementation files. Nothing calls EnsureAllRemotesAsync.

Consequence: on a real machine, the bosun-<hostKey> sftp remote is never created in rclone.conf. Every deep probe (operations/list against that remote) and every mount/mount therefore fails against a real rcd. The tool cannot work at all until this is wired.

It is invisible in tests because the default suite fakes IRcloneClient, so nothing notices the remote does not exist. This is exactly the class of gap that only shows up on first real run - which is also why it should be fixed before that first run rather than discovered during it.

E3 deliberately left the wiring to E5/E7 orchestration (documented in IRcloneRemoteProvisioner's own doc comment) and E5 declined to guess at it. Both were right to flag rather than invent, but the gap is now real and unowned.

What needs deciding as part of the fix:
  - WHEN does EnsureAllRemotesAsync run? Before the supervisor starts probing, certainly. At startup only, or also on config change?
  - What happens if it fails for one host - does that host go Disabled with a surfaced error while others proceed, or is it fatal?
  - How does it interact with bs-127 (RcloneProcessService not registered as a hosted service) and bs-o09 (where hosts.toml lives)? These are one story: what the composition root does at startup, in what order, and how it degrades.

P0 because it blocks the v1 definition of done - item 2 (persistent hosts mount at login) cannot happen without it.
notes: ADR-012 (PROPOSED) drafted covering this, bs-127 and bs-o09 as one startup contract. Awaiting the maintainer decision before any implementation. Nothing has been built against it.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: VERIFY AGAINST REAL RCLONE: is `network_mode` actually honoured by mount/mount? (I7)
description:
The single highest-risk unverified assumption in the codebase right now.

E3 sends network_mode as a FLAT top-level parameter in the mount/mount rc body, and hardcodes it to true so no caller can omit it (Invariant I7). The implementer verified:
  - the general flat-parameter rule at https://rclone.org/rc/#mount-mount ('same names as their CLI flags without -- and with - replaced by _')
  - that mountlib.Options.NetworkMode's Go config tag is literally "network_mode" (pkg.go.dev)
but could NOT find a literal worked example of network_mode in an rc call, the way one exists for vfs_cache_mode. It said so rather than claiming verification. Good.

WHY THIS IS P0 DESPITE BEING A ONE-WORD QUESTION: if the parameter name is wrong, rclone will very likely IGNORE the unknown key rather than error. The mount then succeeds and presents as a FIXED DISK instead of a network drive. Invariant I7 exists because Windows optimises fixed and network drives differently, and presenting an SFTP mount as a fixed disk produces pathological Explorer behaviour. So the failure mode is: everything appears to work, tests are green, and Explorer misbehaves in ways that look like an OS problem rather than a Bosun bug. That is the exact class of failure this project is organised to prevent, and no unit test can catch it - the assertion that network_mode is in the JSON body passes whether or not rclone understands it.

HOW TO VERIFY (needs rclone installed - bs-z8u):
  1. Start rclone rcd on loopback.
  2. Issue a mount/mount with network_mode true, then check the mounted drive's type from Windows - `(Get-PSDrive X).Provider` / `fsutil fsinfo drivetype X:` / Explorer's icon and 'This PC' grouping should show a NETWORK drive, not a fixed disk.
  3. Repeat with the parameter deliberately misspelled. If rclone silently accepts the misspelling and the drive type is identical, that CONFIRMS the silent-failure hypothesis and means we cannot rely on rclone to reject a bad name.
  4. If flat network_mode turns out not to work, switch to the nested mountOpt form and cite the worked example.

Add the result as a marked Integration test so it is checked rather than remembered.

Same verification applies, lower stakes, to config/get's response shape - the implementer inferred it from config/dump and wrote the code to treat any failure as 'not found', so a wrong inference degrades to a redundant config/create rather than a fault.
close_reason: ANSWERED against real rclone v1.75.0 + WinFsp 2.1.25156 and a real SFTP host: mount/mount with network_mode=true yields DriveType=Network, Format=FUSE-rclone. I7 holds. Misspelled parameter is REJECTED with 500, not silently ignored

title: needs-decision: failures_before_unmount has NO validation rule — an I2 hole
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E2. This is the highest-value finding of the night.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md lists no validation rule for failures_before_unmount, so `failures_before_unmount = 0` and negative values are accepted today.

Depending on how E5 writes the comparison, zero means either unmount-on-every-tick, or NEVER UNMOUNT. The latter is a direct Invariant I2 violation: a mounted host whose server dies is never unmounted, the drive letter stays up pointing at nothing, and Explorer wedges process-wide.

This is STRUCTURALLY THE SAME BUG ADR-011 just closed. There, a config value (probe.interval_seconds = 0) could silently disable the unmount path. Here, a different config value can silently disable the same path. ADR-011 fixed one instance; this is the general class, and it suggests the audit is worth completing rather than patching case by case.

Same class, lower stakes, also unvalidated today:
  - probe_timeout_seconds <= 0
  - rclone_rc_port outside 1-65535
  - idle_unmount_seconds negative
  - suspend_unmount_timeout_seconds <= 0 (I8: Windows will not wait forever; a zero budget means never unmounting before sleep)

Recommendation: reject failures_before_unmount < 1, and add positive-range rules for the rest, in docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's validation list and then in ConfigValidator. Every [global] numeric that feeds a safety decision should have a documented range.

The test-author deliberately wrote NO tests for these - inventing validation rules is a spec decision, not an implementation one. That was the right call and it is why this is a decision issue rather than a bug.
close_reason: Validation-completeness audit: numeric ranges added, vfs_cache_mode converted to a case-insensitive allow-list and defaulted in the config layer, network_mode=false rejected. All rules mutation-verified

title: Startup failures before the host is built are logged nowhere
description:
Found while validating E1 (src/Bosun/App.xaml.cs).

App.OnStartup registers the AppDomain and Dispatcher unhandled-exception handlers, then calls BosunHostFactory.CreateHost(), then resolves ILogger<App> into _logger. Both handlers log via `_logger?.` — a null-conditional.

So any exception thrown BEFORE the logger is resolved is swallowed entirely: no file, no debug sink, no window. CreateHost() can genuinely throw here — it calls Directory.CreateDirectory on %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs, which fails on a permissions problem, a redirected/roaming profile, or a full disk. The user would see Bosun fail to start with no diagnostic anywhere, which is the worst possible failure shape for a tray app with no window.

This is not hypothetical for the target environment: docs/DECISIONS.md ADR-010 explicitly courts users on corporate VPNs and domain-joined machines, where redirected AppData is common.

Fix direction: get a minimal bootstrap logger (Serilog self-log, or a file write to a path that cannot fail, or the Windows Event Log) installed BEFORE CreateHost() is called, so the pre-host window is covered. Whatever is chosen must not itself throw.

Acceptance: a test forces CreateHost() to throw (e.g. an unwritable log directory) and asserts a diagnostic is produced somewhere durable.
notes: PROMOTED TO P0 by ADR-012 (rewritten). The startup contract now depends on this in both directions: the catastrophic path needs a MessageBox to appear at a moment when the logger does not yet exist, and every fail-soft path depends on SOMETHING reaching the user. A pre-logger failure that vanishes silently undermines the whole model, so this stops being a nice-to-have.
close_reason: Superseded by bs-ipq (E12a): pre-logger failures now durably recorded via Event Log + fallback file, and terminal ones additionally presented through the catastrophic notifier

title: E2a — Config model types and Tomlyn binding
description:
Immutable model types for config/hosts.toml, bound with Tomlyn.

Shape is docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md exactly: a [global] block, and per-host [hosts.<key>] with nested .mount, .session and .probe tables.

- Records/immutable types; the config is read-only once loaded
- The host's TOML KEY (e.g. `example-nas`) is the stable identity throughout the system. display_name is presentation only. Keep them distinct in the model - a downstream decision (bs-08g) turns on this.
- Global defaults applied when a key is absent, including mounted_probe_interval_seconds = 60 (ADR-011)
- Parse failures surface the TOML line/column; a config error the user cannot locate is a bad error

Do NOT implement validation rules here - that is bs-? (E2b). This issue is parse and bind only.

Acceptance: config/hosts.example.toml parses into the model with every field populated as written, asserted field by field. Malformed TOML produces a diagnostic naming the position.
close_reason: E2 delivered, independently adversarially tested (109 tests), one real bug found and fixed (drive-letter regex anchors)

title: E2c — IHostConfigStore: load, watch, reload, retain-last-valid
description:
The store that owns the live config and its reload lifecycle.

- Load and validate at startup
- Watch config/hosts.toml and re-load on write
- Emit a change event consumers subscribe to
- INVALID CONFIG IS REJECTED WHOLESALE. Never partially applied. The store keeps serving the LAST VALID config and surfaces the error (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6: "Keep running on the last valid config; surface the parse error").
- Debounce/coalesce file writes: editors write in bursts and often truncate-then-write, so a naive watcher fires on a zero-byte intermediate state. Retry a failed read briefly before declaring the config invalid - a transient read failure mid-save is NOT a validation error and must not evict the last valid config.

That debounce point is the subtle part of this issue and the most likely source of a real bug.

Threading: consumers read an immutable snapshot. The store never hands out mutable state.

Acceptance: deterministic tests with an injected filesystem/clock - no Thread.Sleep, no reliance on real FileSystemWatcher timing in unit tests. Cover: valid load; write a valid change and observe the event; write an invalid change and assert the PREVIOUS config is still served and an error surfaced; simulate a truncated mid-write read and assert the last valid config survives.
close_reason: E2 delivered, independently adversarially tested (109 tests), one real bug found and fixed (drive-letter regex anchors)

title: E2b — Config validation rules
description:
Every validation rule in docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md, each producing a distinct, locatable error.

Rules (reject the WHOLE config if any fail):
- duplicate host key or duplicate display_name
- two hosts claiming the same drive letter
- mode != "none" with no drive or no remote_path
- drive not matching ^[D-Z]:$ (A-C reserved)
- vfs_cache_mode in {off, minimal}
- identity_file path does not resolve to an existing file
- backoff_seconds empty or containing non-positive values
- probe.interval_seconds negative
- global.mounted_probe_interval_seconds zero or negative (ABSENT IS NOT AN ERROR - defaults to 60, ADR-011)

Why each matters, so you can judge edge cases: duplicate display_name is not cosmetic - E7 emits Terminal profiles named from it, and `wt -p "<name>"` has undocumented tie-breaking on collisions, so uniqueness here is what makes profile launching deterministic. vfs_cache_mode below writes breaks editors and Office outright (Invariant I6). Drive collisions must never be auto-resolved (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6).

Validation must be a pure function over the parsed model - no I/O except the identity_file existence check, which must be injectable so tests do not depend on the developer's ~/.ssh contents.

Acceptance: one test per rule, each failing for exactly one describable reason. A config violating two rules reports both, not just the first. A valid config produces no errors.
notes:
ADR-011 acceptance criteria absorbed from bs-ugm (superseded):
- A config OMITTING mounted_probe_interval_seconds parses and yields 60. Absent is NOT an error.
- mounted_probe_interval_seconds = 0 is rejected; the previous config is retained.
- mounted_probe_interval_seconds negative is rejected.
- probe.interval_seconds negative is rejected.
- probe.interval_seconds = 0 PARSES - it is the documented on-demand default (ADR-008) and must not be rejected.
The binding and the default-60 behaviour belong to bs-0na (E2a); the two rejection rules belong here.
close_reason: E2 delivered, independently adversarially tested (109 tests), one real bug found and fixed (drive-letter regex anchors)

title: E5 — Mount supervisor: the state machine
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E5. THE CORE OF THE PROJECT — build and test this before any UI.

- State machine exactly as specified in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4
- Single-threaded async loop; per-host transitions serialised through one channel
- Reconciliation against mount/listmounts every tick
- Adopt-or-clear existing mounts on startup (crash recovery)
- Idle-unmount timer for on-demand hosts
- Forced-unmount escalation when a clean unmount does not confirm
- Extensive unit tests on the transition table: every transition, every guard, every timeout path
