title: Probe mounted hosts even when interval_seconds = 0 (ADR-011)
description:
Implement the ADR-011 probe-scheduling split in the supervisor.

Rule (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 rule 3):
- probe.interval_seconds governs polling while a host is IDLE (Ready, Unreachable) only. 0 = do not poll while idle.
- A host in Mounted is ALWAYS probed. Effective interval:
    interval_seconds > 0  → min(interval_seconds, global.mounted_probe_interval_seconds)
    interval_seconds == 0 → global.mounted_probe_interval_seconds

Why this exists: without it, an on-demand host with interval_seconds = 0 (the documented default, and what config/hosts.example.toml ships for example-remote) is never probed once mounted, so it never accumulates failures, never reaches Draining, and leaves a drive letter pointing at a dead host. That is an Invariant I2 violation and the exact wedged-Explorer failure the project exists to prevent.

Acceptance criteria:
- A mounted host with interval_seconds = 0 is probed at mounted_probe_interval_seconds and reaches Draining after failures_before_unmount consecutive failures.
- A host with interval_seconds = 3600 is probed at mounted_probe_interval_seconds while mounted (clamped), not at 3600.
- A host with interval_seconds = 15 is probed at 15 while mounted (not clamped up).
- An on-demand host in Ready with interval_seconds = 0 generates NO probe traffic — the ADR-008 behaviour must not regress.
- Tests are deterministic with injected time; no sleeps, no real clock, fake IProbe.
notes:
VALIDATION FINDING from the orchestrator (mutation testing, 2026-08-16):

The implementation of ADR-011 is CORRECT. The TEST guarding it is weaker than its name.

I replaced EffectiveMountedProbeIntervalSeconds with `return interval;` -- i.e. reverted to the
pre-ADR-011 behaviour where interval 0 means "never probe". Only ONE test failed
(Mounted_host_with_long_interval_is_clamped_to_mounted_probe_interval).

The test named Mounted_host_with_interval_zero_is_probed_at_mounted_probe_interval_and_reaches_Draining
PASSED under that mutation. It advances 60s three times and asserts failures accumulate and an
unmount happens; with interval 0 the timer fires about once per advance anyway, so the observable
outcome is identical. It proves the host DRAINS. It does not prove the CADENCE is
mounted_probe_interval_seconds.

That test is named for the project's most important invariant and would not catch its own
regression. The independent test-author has been briefed to pin cadence precisely: advancing just
under the interval must produce ZERO probes, advancing to exactly the interval must produce EXACTLY
ONE. Assert probe counts and timing, not eventual state.

Keeping this issue open until that stronger test lands.
close_reason: ADR-011 scheduling implemented; cadence now pinned by independent boundary tests (59s->0 probes, 60s->1), replacing the weaker drains-eventually assertion

title: E6 spec gaps: resume vs network asymmetry, undocumented debounce, 8s vs 2s budget
description:
Six ambiguities surfaced by independent adversarial testing of E6. Each needs a sentence in the spec rather than an inference in the code.

1. §3's RESUME row and §6's failure row CONTRADICT. Network change gets 're-probe all immediately; force-probe mounted hosts'; resume gets only 're-probe all immediately' - and the implementation read that asymmetry as 'resume touches no mounted host at all', while §6 demands force-unmount AND reconcile on resume. Resume is the more dangerous transition of the two. One row is wrong. This is the root cause of the resume bug.

2. THE NETWORK DEBOUNCE IS UNDOCUMENTED AND UNBOUNDED. 750ms is a private constant in Win32SystemEventSource; neither ARCHITECTURE.md nor CONFIG-SCHEMA.md mentions a debounce at all, so §3's 're-probe all immediately' now means '750ms after the network settles'. Because it is purely trailing-edge with NO MAXIMUM DEFERRAL, a link flapping faster than the window defers the event INDEFINITELY. Given that network interruption is one of the maintainer's two real failure modes, an unbounded deferral on a flapping link is precisely the case that matters. Probably needs a cap, and certainly needs documenting.

3. THE 8s DEFAULT CONTRADICTS THE ADAPTER'S OWN 2s FIGURE. SystemEventSupervisorAdapter's remarks say Windows allows 'roughly two seconds'; DefaultSuspendUnmountTimeoutSeconds is 8. If 2s is right, the default blocks SystemEvents' single process-wide notification thread for four times longer than Windows will wait - delaying delivery to every other subscriber in the process, for nothing. One of the two numbers should change.

4. A HOST ALREADY DRAINING WHEN SUSPEND ARRIVES IS UNSPECIFIED. SuspendAsync sweeps only Mounted/Mounting (matching rule 5's letter), so a host mid-drain for an ordinary reason keeps the 10s DrainConfirmTimeout rather than the suspend budget, and may schedule its escalation past the moment the machine sleeps.

5. WHAT THE SUSPEND HANDLER SHOULD DO WITH A SUPERVISOR FAULT is unspecified - see the process-termination bug.

6. A USER-MOUNTED ON-DEMAND HOST DOES NOT SURVIVE A SLEEP, and no ADR covers it. Current behaviour returns it to Ready per rule 6, which is the correct reading of the spec as written. But ADR-015 reasoned at length about not undoing an explicit user UNMOUNT; the mirror case - a suspend undoing an explicit user MOUNT twenty minutes earlier - has no decision recorded. ADR-015's Consequences already flag the Disabled-state conflation as the underlying cause.

title: Rewrite the manual test protocol around the hardware that actually exists
description:
Supersedes bs-xd6's assumptions. docs/OPERATIONS.md's protocol is written for a laptop that docks and moves; the maintainer has a Windows DESKTOP and a Mac laptop, so T2 as written - "Close the lid. Move to a different network. Open." - cannot be run at all, and it is the test CLAUDE.md §7 calls the one that matters.

The scenarios that actually occur, in his words, are OVERNIGHT SLEEP and NETWORK INTERRUPTION.

Rewrite T1-T3 around those:

  T1 - Overnight sleep, host still reachable. Persistent mount up; sleep the desktop overnight; wake. PASS: Explorer responsive immediately, and the drive either works or is cleanly gone and remounting. This is a HARDER test than the old T2, because the host is still up: the shallow probe passes while the mount may be dead (see the dead-mount bug).

  T2 - Network interruption shorter than the unmount threshold. Unplug the switch / drop the link for less time than failures_before_unmount x interval, restore it. PASS: Explorer responsive, drive usable or cleanly replaced. Catches the same dead-mount case without needing to sleep.

  T3 - Host dies while mounted. Keep roughly as-is; power off the NAS or drop its NIC. This one already matches reality.

Keep T4 (drag and drop), T5 (idle unmount), T6 (crash recovery) - all hardware-agnostic.

Add a row on reading the transition log, since that is the artifact that explains a result after the fact, and it is where the trigger for each transition is recorded.

Do not fabricate results. Write the protocol; leave results empty until a run happens. traininggrounds (192.168.0.144, LAN) is the natural subject.

title: E6a — ISystemEventSource: power, network, session-switch wrappers
description:
The seam around three .NET event sources (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3):

  Microsoft.Win32.SystemEvents.PowerModeChanged   -> Suspend / Resume
  System.Net.NetworkInformation.NetworkChange.NetworkAddressChanged
  Microsoft.Win32.SystemEvents.SessionSwitch      -> SessionLock (v1: NO ACTION, reserved)

One interface, one Win32 implementation, one fake. No test in the default suite may subscribe to a real system event - they fire on the OS's schedule, not the test's, which is the definition of non-deterministic.

THINGS THAT WILL BITE:
  - SystemEvents requires a message pump. A WPF app has one, but SystemEvents raises handlers on its OWN dedicated thread, not the UI thread, and a handler that blocks it stalls every other subscriber in the process.
  - SystemEvents holds handlers via a static event. Failing to unsubscribe leaks the object for the process lifetime; unsubscribe on dispose and prove it in a test.
  - NetworkAddressChanged fires SEVERAL TIMES for one physical transition (adapter down, DHCP, adapter up). Docking a laptop can produce a burst. Coalescing belongs here or in E6b - decide which, and say why.

Acceptance: the fake drives every event type deterministically; the real implementation is exercised only by a marked integration test the human runs; disposal unsubscribes and is asserted.
close_reason: E6 delivered and validated: 506/506, suspend budget mutation-verified (removing it hangs the tests, exactly the production failure), no default-suite test touches a real system event

title: E6b — The adapter: translate system events into supervisor calls, within the time budget
description:
Wire ISystemEventSource to IMountSupervisor. The supervisor already has SuspendAsync, ResumeAsync and NetworkChangedAsync (E5) - this epic is the ADAPTER that calls them, not new state-machine logic. Do not add transitions.

  Suspend        -> IMountSupervisor.SuspendAsync, BOUNDED by global.suspend_unmount_timeout_seconds
  Resume         -> IMountSupervisor.ResumeAsync (re-probe all, bypass backoff)
  NetworkChanged -> IMountSupervisor.NetworkChangedAsync (reset backoff, force-probe)
  SessionLock    -> nothing in v1. Wire the event, log it, take no action.

INVARIANT I8 AND THE HARD PART. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3: 'The suspend handler must complete quickly. Windows does not wait indefinitely.' In practice that window is nearer TWO SECONDS than the 8s default, which is why bs-ajh exists. The handler must:
  - block the suspend only as long as the budget allows, and never longer;
  - not deadlock if the supervisor's command channel is busy - SuspendAsync posts to the same single channel everything else uses, so a slow drain in flight could otherwise hold the machine awake or, worse, return after Windows has stopped waiting;
  - accept that a forced unmount may still be needed on resume, and say so in the log rather than pretending the drain completed.

Every transition already logs host, from-state, to-state and trigger. Make the TRIGGER for these read unambiguously as the system event, because docs/OPERATIONS.md's whole triage story for T1-T3 is reading that log after the fact.

Register in the ADR-012 startup sequence. System events should be subscribed AFTER the supervisor is running - an event arriving before it is ready has nothing to act on.

Acceptance: fake events drive real supervisor calls; the suspend path is proven to return within budget even when the channel is busy; SessionLock provably does nothing.
close_reason: E6 delivered and validated: 506/506, suspend budget mutation-verified (removing it hangs the tests, exactly the production failure), no default-suite test touches a real system event

title: Wire FragmentRewriteCoordinator into the startup sequence
description:
FragmentRewriteCoordinator is built and tested but is NOT wired into BosunHostFactory or StartupOrchestrator, so the fragment is never written or rewritten in production yet.

The implementer flagged rather than guessed, for a good reason: StartupOrchestrator's own doc comment (ADR-012) is explicit that IHostConfigStore may only be resolved via IServiceProvider, inside a try/catch, by that ONE class - because its factory does real file I/O and throws on an invalid first load. An independently-registered IHostedService taking IHostConfigStore by constructor injection would have DI activate it OUTSIDE that try/catch and defeat the guarantee.

So this is the same ordering question ADR-012 answered for rclone and the supervisor, now for the fragment writer. Where does fragment writing join the sequence?

Worth noting it is NOT gated on WinFsp or rclone: Terminal profiles are the half of Bosun that works when mounting cannot (ADR-012's whole degradation model rests on that). Writing the fragment should therefore happen EARLY - right after config loads - and should not be skipped when later steps fail. On a machine with no WinFsp, the profiles are the entire value the user gets.

Also decide: rewrite on ConfigChanged is implemented in the coordinator, but bs-7ck notes MountSupervisor does not react to ConfigChanged either. These are the same unfinished thought - config reload is wired to nothing today.
close_reason: Fragment writer wired early and ungated; tmux_session validation added; reconnect loop capped. All mutation-verified; the errorlevel diagnosis was corrected and independently confirmed (9009 vs >= semantics)

title: needs-decision: the reconnect wrapper retries forever if ssh cannot be launched at all
description:
Found by the E7 implementer, and verified EMPIRICALLY against a real cmd.exe rather than reasoned about - good work.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md specifies session.reconnect as a loop that retries on exit code 255 (dropped) and exits cleanly on 0 (user typed exit). E7 implements that as:

    cmd.exe /d /c "for /l %n in (1,0,2) do (<ssh invocation> & if not errorlevel 255 exit /b)"

Verified working for both documented codes. But there is a third case the schema never considered.

If ssh.exe CANNOT BE LAUNCHED AT ALL - not on PATH - cmd.exe prints "is not recognized as an internal or external command" and DOES NOT MOVE %errorlevel%. It stays at whatever it was before. So `if not errorlevel 255` tests a stale value and the loop spins forever, with no error surfaced and no bound.

This is the same SHAPE as bs-k4k (unbounded retry against a permanent failure), in a different layer - and unlike bs-k4k it burns in a Terminal tab the user is watching, so it is at least visible. But it produces a tab that scrolls errors forever rather than telling the user what is wrong.

Narrow: ssh ships with Windows and being on PATH is already a documented prerequisite. Real nonetheless, and cheap to close.

Options:
  A. Cap the retries (a counted loop rather than an infinite one), then exit with a message naming the last exit code. Bounded, self-explaining.
  B. Probe for ssh once before the loop and fail immediately with an actionable message if it is missing.
  C. Leave it; document the prerequisite harder.

Recommendation: A, and mention the cap in docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's session.reconnect row. A loop that gives up and says why is strictly better than one that cannot, and it costs a counter.

The implementer deliberately did NOT invent a cap, because CONFIG-SCHEMA specifies only the two-code contract and CLAUDE.md §5 says to file rather than guess. Correct call.
notes:
DIAGNOSIS CORRECTED, and the implementer''s version is better than the one this issue was filed with.

I hypothesised that cmd.exe does not move %errorlevel% for a not-recognized command. WRONG. Verified
independently: cmd.exe DOES set errorlevel to 9009.

The actual mechanism is that `if errorlevel N` tests `>=`, not `==`. So `if not errorlevel 255`
means "exit when errorlevel < 255" -- and 9009 >= 255, so it takes the RETRY branch. Confirmed by
direct probe: `WOULD-RETRY lvl=9009`.

This matters because it makes the bug BROADER than "ssh is missing": ANY exit code at or above 255
loops forever. 9009 (not recognized) is one case; a process killed by an access violation
(-1073741819, huge unsigned) is another. ssh itself uses 255 for its own errors and 0-254 to relay
the remote command''s status, so codes above 255 always come from Windows rather than ssh.

The cap fixes it regardless of cause, which is the right shape: it does not depend on enumerating
which exit codes are pathological.

Two further cmd.exe findings the implementer confirmed empirically, both load-bearing for the fix:
  - In a single-line `cmd /c "..."` (not a .bat), plain %errorlevel% is substituted ONCE at parse
    time, so it is always stale. `if errorlevel N` is unaffected (runtime builtin), but printing the
    value needs delayed expansion (/v:on and !errorlevel!).
  - An un-parenthesized `if cond action & next` in that context does NOT run `next` unconditionally
    the way it would in a .bat file -- a false condition swallows everything chained after `&`.

Both are the kind of thing only running cmd.exe reveals.
close_reason: Fragment writer wired early and ungated; tmux_session validation added; reconnect loop capped. All mutation-verified; the errorlevel diagnosis was corrected and independently confirmed (9009 vs >= semantics)

title: E7b — Profile generation from host config
description:
Map each configured host to a Terminal profile. Pure function from config to model; no filesystem.

COMMANDLINE (ADR-013 - the config KEY, not display_name, not user@hostname):
    ssh <config-key>                                  # tmux = false
    ssh -t <config-key> tmux new -A -s <session>      # tmux = true

The key form is deliberate: a fully-specified `ssh -i <key> -p <port> <user>@<host>` would not match a `Host <alias>` block in the user's ssh_config, silently discarding ProxyJump and everything else configured there. ADR-010 courts users with bastion hosts.

RECONNECT WRAPPER (session.reconnect = true): wrap the invocation in a loop that retries on exit code 255 (dropped) but exits cleanly on 0 (user typed `exit`). docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md is explicit about those two codes. Note the interaction with E8: SshCommandLineParser reads the ssh.exe process's OWN command line, which the wrapper does not change - but verify that assumption holds for whatever wrapper form is chosen, and say so.

COLOURS: tab_color and color_scheme pass through from config. color_scheme is referenced BY NAME only - Bosun never defines a scheme (bs-289).

HOSTS WITH mode = "none" STILL GET A PROFILE. The terminal and mount axes are independent (ADR-008); a jump host is shell-only and is exactly the case that must work.

CROSS-EPIC CONTRACT TEST, cheap and important: feed the commandline this produces through E8's SshCommandLineParser and assert it correlates back to the right config key. E7 and E8 were built independently against the same ambiguous spec line; that test IS the contract.

Acceptance: one profile per configured host including mode=none; both commandline forms; reconnect wrapper; the E8 round-trip test.
close_reason: E7 delivered and independently validated: 462/462, published GUID vector reproduced by an INDEPENDENT implementation, encoding mutation-tested, E7/E8 contract test passing

title: E7c — IFragmentWriter: path resolution, atomic write, rewrite on config change
description:
The filesystem half.

VERIFIED PATH (research on bs-3ir, primary-sourced from Microsoft Learn):
    %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\bosun.json
NOTE the `Microsoft\` segment - ADR-006 and CLAUDE.md I5 both abbreviate it away. The path must be INJECTABLE; no test may write the real one.

Also verified and worth knowing: the Store-vs-unpackaged distinction in ADR-006's note is a red herring. Both the ProgramData and LocalAppData Fragments directories are read regardless of how Terminal was installed; the Store distinction applies only to Store-PACKAGED APPS registering via an app-extension manifest, which an unpackaged win-x64 exe does not use.

INVARIANT I5: never read, write, or merge the user's settings.json. Not to check whether a scheme exists, not to detect anything. The fragment is the only file Bosun touches.

- Write atomically (temp file + move). A half-written fragment is invalid JSON, and Terminal skips a malformed fragment SILENTLY - no toast, no error, no log (verified; see bs-3ir). A torn write would look exactly like Bosun having done nothing.
- Create the directory if absent; the installer is expected to.
- Rewrite on IHostConfigStore.ConfigChanged.
- Validate our own output before writing - since Terminal will not tell us it was rejected, the only defence is not producing invalid output in the first place.

Acceptance: writes to an INJECTED temp path; output parses as JSON; a simulated mid-write failure leaves the previous fragment intact; a test asserts the writer never opens a path containing settings.json.
close_reason: E7 delivered and independently validated: 462/462, published GUID vector reproduced by an INDEPENDENT implementation, encoding mutation-tested, E7/E8 contract test passing

title: E7a — Fragment model, profile GUID derivation, and serialisation
description:
The data half of the fragment writer. Pure, fully unit-testable, no filesystem.

- Fragment document model matching Terminal's schema: a top-level object with a `profiles` array. Do NOT emit a `schemes` array (bs-289: reference existing scheme names only; shipping our own risks colliding in Terminal's single global scheme namespace, and collision behaviour is undocumented).
- Profile fields: name, guid, commandline, startingDirectory, icon, colorScheme, tabColor.
- SET startingDirectory EXPLICITLY. Terminal's docs self-contradict on its default (they state %USERPROFILE% then list four launch-context-dependent values), so relying on the default is relying on something undocumented.

PROFILE GUID (ADR-013, verified research on bs-3ir). Terminal derives a fragment profile's GUID as:
    appNamespace = UUIDv5(TERMINAL_FRAGMENT_NS, app-name)
    profileGuid  = UUIDv5(appNamespace, profile-name)
  TERMINAL_FRAGMENT_NS = {f65ddb7e-706b-4499-8a50-40313caf510a}
  Name strings are encoded UTF-16LE before hashing.

Bosun emits the guid EXPLICITLY, derived from the host's CONFIG KEY rather than display_name - otherwise renaming display_name makes Terminal see a brand-new profile and silently orphans the user's per-profile customisation (ADR-013).

Microsoft publishes a worked test vector: app "Git", profile "Git Bash" -> {2ece5bfe-50ed-5f3a-ab87-5cd4baafed2b}. USE IT AS A UNIT TEST. If the derivation reproduces that, the implementation is right; if it does not, nothing else in this epic matters.

Acceptance: the test vector reproduces exactly; serialisation round-trips; output is valid JSON.
close_reason: E7 delivered and independently validated: 462/462, published GUID vector reproduced by an INDEPENDENT implementation, encoding mutation-tested, E7/E8 contract test passing

title: Implement BOTH halves of ADR-014 together — tier-split polling and rule 8
description:
Found by the agent implementing the mounting-availability gate, while reading the surrounding code.

ADR-014 rule 8 (ratified 2026-08-16, and now written into docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4) says:

  "RequestMountAsync on an Unreachable host triggers an immediate probe and proceeds to mount if it
   passes. It is never a silent no-op."

That is NOT implemented. RequestMountAsync delegates straight into TryBeginMountAsync, whose first
guard is `if (host.State != MountState.Ready) { LogDebug(...); return; }` - so a mount click on an
Unreachable host still logs at Debug and returns, which is the exact behaviour ADR-014 was written
to eliminate.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: ADR-014 ALSO stopped the backoff ladder from polling on-demand
hosts while Unreachable. Those two halves were adopted as a pair. With rule 8 missing, an on-demand
host whose server is off is now never re-polled AND cannot be mounted by clicking - so it can never
leave Unreachable by any route at all. The ADR's own reasoning names this as the failure it was
avoiding, and implementing one half without the other produces precisely it.

NOTE the existing Independent test A_user_mount_request_for_an_unreachable_host_issues_no_deep_probe_and_no_mount
is consistent with EITHER reading, because its shallow probe is scripted to fail - so nothing
currently exercises the "immediate probe" itself. Worth strengthening alongside the fix.

FIX: RequestMountAsync on an Unreachable host performs a shallow probe immediately; on success the
host moves to Ready and the normal mount path proceeds (which then applies rule 1's deep probe and
the bs-yvw.1 availability gate, both unchanged). On failure it reports why, rather than returning
silently.

Interacts with bs-yvw.1: if mounting is unavailable process-wide, RequestMountAsync now throws
MountingUnavailableException with the causal reason BEFORE any of this, which is correct - telling
the user "WinFsp is not installed" beats probing a host we could not mount anyway.
notes:
CORRECTION (orchestrator, after actually reading ArmIdleProbeTimer rather than asserting from memory):

This issue originally claimed that with rule 8 missing, an on-demand host "is never re-polled AND
cannot be mounted by clicking - so it can never leave Unreachable by any route at all." THAT IS
WRONG as the code stands.

ArmIdleProbeTimer currently arms the backoff ladder for ANY Unreachable host regardless of tier, so
an on-demand host IS still re-polled and CAN recover on its own. No deadlock exists today.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: NEITHER half of ADR-014 is implemented. E5 predates the ADR and nobody has
been back since.
  - ADR-014: ladder polls PERSISTENT hosts only while Unreachable. Code polls ALL of them.
  - ADR-014 rule 8: mount click on an Unreachable host probes immediately. Code logs at Debug and
    returns.

So today an on-demand host generates ladder traffic while its server is off (contradicting ADR-011's
"no traffic until the user mounts one"), and the tray's Mount click on it silently does nothing.

THE REAL HAZARD IS ORDERING, and it is worth stating loudly because the trap is live:

The tier-split is the OBVIOUS half to implement - a one-line conditional in ArmIdleProbeTimer,
exactly the sort of thing picked up as a quick win. Implementing that half ALONE creates the
deadlock this issue originally (incorrectly) described: the host stops being polled, rule 1 forbids
Mounting from anywhere but Ready, and the mount click is still a no-op - so it can never leave
Unreachable by any route.

=> BOTH HALVES MUST LAND IN THE SAME CHANGE. Do not split this issue.
close_reason: Both halves of ADR-014 landed together: tier-split ladder and rule 8, mutation-verified including the deadlock guard. Resume/network-change deliberately NOT tier-split; §4 amended

title: Verify config/create and mount/listmounts parameter shapes against real rclone
description:
rclone v1.75.0 is now installed, and RcloneProcessIntegrationTests proves a real rcd starts and answers core/version. That makes two MORE rc endpoints verifiable against the real binary without needing WinFsp or a reachable SFTP host:

  * config/create - writes a remote into rclone.conf. Needs no network and no WinFsp. Verifiable end to end: create a bosun-<key> sftp remote against a TEMPORARY rclone.conf, then read it back with config/get and assert the parameter names landed as intended (host, port, user, key_file, ask_password).
  * mount/listmounts - should return an empty list on a clean rcd. Verifies the response SHAPE (Fs, MountPoint, MountedOn) that E5's reconciliation and the bs-ka9 Fs-aware adoption both depend on.

WHY THIS MATTERS: CLAUDE.md names rc parameter names as one of two areas where secondhand information is routinely wrong, and E3 flagged config/get's response shape as INFERRED rather than verified (it was inferred from config/dump; no literal worked example exists). This closes that gap for real, and it is the same class of risk as bs-1sy - a wrong parameter name that rclone silently ignores rather than rejecting.

CONSTRAINTS: marked [Trait(TestCategories.Category, TestCategories.Integration)] so it stays out of the default suite and out of CI. It MUST use a temporary rclone.conf path, never the user's real %APPDATA%\rclone\rclone.conf - clobbering the maintainer's own remotes would be a genuinely damaging test. And it must not attempt mount/mount, which needs WinFsp.

Still blocked and NOT part of this: mount/mount and network_mode (bs-1sy, bs-dtk - need WinFsp), operations/list (needs a reachable SFTP host).
close_reason: Verified against real rclone v1.75.0: config/get returns exactly the flat key:value shape E3 inferred (gap closed, no client change needed); mount/listmounts envelope confirmed. Surfaced the 403 auth defect as a separate P0

title: E12c — Config at %LOCALAPPDATA% and first-run bootstrap (bs-o09)
description:
ADR-012 Decision 4: configuration lives at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\hosts.toml, symmetric with the log path.

- Change BosunHostOptions.CreateDefault(). The repo-relative path survives ONLY as a dev override through the already-injected option.
- First run creates the directory and writes a template derived from config/hosts.example.toml. Do NOT ship a config with example hosts enabled - a template that would try to mount nas.example.internal on first launch is worse than no config.
- FileSystemConfigWatcher's constructor currently throws if its directory does not exist. It must tolerate a directory that was created a moment ago, or the bootstrap order must guarantee creation first. Either is fine; be explicit about which.
- Update docs/OPERATIONS.md so it can say 'your configuration and your logs are both under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun'.

NOTE the ADR-012 distinction: NO CONFIG AT ALL IS NOT A FAILURE. It is first run, the expected path for a fresh install, and gets a window shown actively rather than a warning. The window itself is E9 work (bs-ww9.1); this issue provides the detection and the template, and must expose 'no configuration present' as a distinct readiness state, not as an error.

Acceptance: fresh-profile simulation with an injected filesystem root - directory created, template written, watcher starts, readiness reports 'awaiting first-run configuration' rather than a fault.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: E9 must render degraded startup state causally (from ADR-012)
description:
Two obligations ADR-012 places on E9, which must be in its brief BEFORE it is written rather than retrofitted.

1. THE TRAY ICON ENCODES AGGREGATE HEALTH AT A GLANCE. A degraded Bosun must not look identical to a healthy one. Not a tooltip - nobody hovers. Every other channel (toast, dialog, log) is a one-shot the user can miss, so the icon is the only always-on surface. This is what makes fail-soft defensible at all.

2. NOTIFICATIONS AND THE STATUS WINDOW MUST BE CAUSAL. 'P: is not mounted - WinFsp is not installed', not 'some features unavailable'. A user who configured a persistent mount and finds no drive letter will otherwise blame Windows, the VPN, or the network, and burn twenty minutes before suspecting the tray app sitting there looking healthy. Degradation that does not explain itself actively misdirects.

Also from ADR-012: the first-run case (no config at all) is a WINDOW shown actively, not a warning - it is the expected path for a fresh install, not a fault.

Blocked on bs-98w (ratify ADR-012).
notes: ADDITIONAL E9 obligation from ADR-015: the tray must distinguish PARKED from UNREACHABLE from MOUNTED. A user who deliberately unmounted a drive should see that they parked it - a drive that is deliberately absent must not look like a drive that broke. Joins the ADR-012 requirement that the icon and status window explain state causally rather than generically.

title: needs-decision: ADR-011 contradicts §4 Backoff for Unreachable hosts, and mount-from-Unreachable is undefined
description:
Found by INDEPENDENT adversarial testing of E5. A sharp one, and it touches the ADR we wrote last night.

THE CONTRADICTION. ADR-011 rule 1 says probe.interval_seconds governs polling while a host is IDLE, naming both Ready AND Unreachable, and that 0 means do not poll while idle. Its Consequence paragraph is blunter still: 'On-demand hosts generate no traffic until the user mounts one.'

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 Backoff says Unreachable -> Probing uses the backoff ladder, unconditionally, with no exemption for interval_seconds = 0.

The implementation follows §4 and polls an interval=0 on-demand host every 300s forever while its server is off. That contradicts ADR-011's stated consequence.

WHY THE LITERAL ADR-011 READING IS WORSE, AND WHY NO FAILING TEST WAS WRITTEN FOR IT: if an Unreachable host with interval_seconds = 0 is never re-polled, it can never reach Ready. Transition rule 1 forbids Mounting from anywhere except Ready. So the tray's 'mount' click on that host becomes a PERMANENT NO-OP - the user clicks, nothing happens, forever, with no error. That is worse than a little background traffic. The test author declined to encode either behaviour and escalated instead, which was right.

SO THE REAL QUESTION IS: what should RequestMountAsync do when the host is Unreachable? Today it silently logs at Debug and returns. The spec says nothing.

Options:
  A. RequestMountAsync on an Unreachable host triggers an immediate probe, and mounts if it passes. Honours rule 1 (still no mount without a passing probe) AND honours the user's click. Then ADR-011's 'no traffic while idle' can hold literally, because the user's action is what generates the traffic. This is the orchestrator's recommendation - it resolves the contradiction and the dead-click together.
  B. Keep polling Unreachable hosts on the ladder regardless of interval_seconds, and amend ADR-011's Consequence paragraph to admit it. Simple, costs a probe every 300s per down host.
  C. Poll Unreachable on the ladder only for hosts whose mode is persistent; on-demand hosts stay dark until clicked, with option A's behaviour on click.

Recommendation: A plus C. On-demand hosts generate no traffic until acted on, which is what ADR-008 and ADR-011 both promise, and clicking mount does the obvious thing.

Whichever is chosen, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 must define RequestMountAsync's behaviour from Unreachable, because 'silently does nothing' is not a defensible answer for a tray menu item.
close_reason: ADR-014: ladder polls persistent hosts only; on-demand stay dark; RequestMountAsync from Unreachable probes immediately

title: needs-decision: should a user-requested unmount of a PERSISTENT host stick?
description:
Surfaced by the E5 implementer, which wrote a test named Persistent_host_remounts_itself_after_a_user_requested_unmount specifically to make the behaviour VISIBLE rather than let it be a silent surprise. Good instinct; the behaviour still needs a decision.

Current behaviour: every drain routes through Disabled, then auto-re-arms to Probing unless the host is administratively disabled or the system is suspended. So a persistent host the user unmounts from the tray drains, re-probes, and REMOUNTS ITSELF within a probe interval.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 rule 6 carves out on-demand hosts only ('On-demand hosts rest in Ready, not Mounted. They do not auto-mount.'). It says nothing about a user-initiated unmount of a persistent host, so the current behaviour is a defensible reading of the spec as written.

But it is probably not what a user means. Clicking 'unmount' and watching the drive come back a minute later reads as the tool ignoring you, and it is the kind of thing that produces a bug report rather than a shrug. There are legitimate reasons to want it gone temporarily - copying a large file locally, a flaky link, wanting Explorer quiet.

Options:
  A. A user-requested unmount sets a sticky 'suppressed' flag on that host, cleared by an explicit user remount, by config reload, or by app restart. Persistent tier resumes automatically after those events, not before.
  B. Keep current behaviour and make the UI honest - the tray says 'unmount (will remount when reachable)'. Cheap but unsatisfying.
  C. User unmount implies administratively Disabled until re-enabled - strongest, but then the persistent tier stops meaning much for that host until the user remembers.

Recommendation: A. It matches what the click means, it is recoverable by obvious actions, and it does not weaken the persistent tier's automatic behaviour in any case the user did not explicitly ask for.

Whatever is chosen, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 should say it explicitly, since the current silence is what produced the ambiguity.
notes:
STRENGTHENED by independent adversarial testing (2026-08-16). The test author derived "stays down"
from docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 read as a whole, and the argument is stronger than my original framing:

  - "user unmount" is listed as a Mounted -> Draining trigger
  - the ONLY edge out of Draining is -> Disabled
  - the ONLY edge out of Disabled is "enable"
  - Disabled's only annotation on the diagram is "user disables"

So the diagram already says a user unmount ends PARKED. Rule 6 governs a tier's RESTING state, not
the override of an explicit command, and ADR-005 concerns probe failure - it says nothing about
undoing a deliberate user instruction.

Also noted: `Disabled` currently conflates three distinct things - never-enabled (mode = none),
parked-by-suspend, and drained-and-about-to-re-enable. That conflation is WHY this bug exists. A
distinct parked state, or an AdministrativelyEnabled flag the user unmount clears, would make rule 6
decidable rather than ambiguous.

I have had this implemented as "stays unmounted" (the spec-supported reading), with the mechanism
deliberately easy to invert and the parked state visible in the tray snapshot, so a drive that stays
gone does not look like a fault. Reverse it here if you disagree.
close_reason: ADR-015: user unmount parks the host until explicit remount, config reload, or restart; parked hosts keep probing. Ratifies the behaviour already shipped in E5; §4 rule 9 added

title: Wire RcloneProcessService as a hosted service and decide startup ordering
description:
E3 built, tested and registered RcloneProcessService as a resolvable singleton but deliberately did NOT register it via AddHostedService, and said so rather than doing it quietly.

Reason: doing so would make every host.StartAsync() force-resolve IHostConfigStore in order to build RcloneProcessServiceOptions from global.rclone_rc_port / rclone_config_path. That breaks the deliberately-lazy config-load pattern E1 established, which BosunHostFactoryTests.Host_StartsAndStopsCleanlyWithoutAWindow explicitly relies on (it starts a host whose ConfigPath does not point at a real file).

So there is a genuine startup-ordering question to settle, and it belongs with whoever owns the composition root:
  - When does the config load, relative to starting rclone rcd?
  - What happens when the config is INVALID at startup? HostConfigStore.Load throws by design (no previous config to fall back to). Does Bosun refuse to start entirely, or start with mounts disabled and terminal features working - the same graceful degradation E3 already implements for missing WinFsp?
  - When does IRcloneRemoteProvisioner.EnsureAllRemotesAsync run relative to process start and first probe?

The WinFsp-absent path already establishes the principle: DEGRADE, do not fail - a user without WinFsp still gets their Terminal profiles. An invalid config arguably deserves the same treatment rather than a hard startup failure, but that is a decision, not an implementation detail.

Related: bs-o09 (where hosts.toml lives) and bs-16b (startup failures before the logger exists are currently logged nowhere - which would make a hard startup failure invisible). These three are the same story and are probably best decided together.
notes: Folded into ADR-012 (PROPOSED). The lazy-config objection recorded here is addressed there: it is a test concern that leaked into production design, and the recommendation is to fix the test (build the host without the startup orchestrator) rather than keep production lazy.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: E3a — RcloneProcessService: own the rclone rcd lifetime
description:
One long-lived `rclone rcd` child process, started at launch and stopped cleanly at exit (ADR-003, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2).

- Start on a configurable LOOPBACK port (global.rclone_rc_port, default 5572). Never bind a non-loopback interface - the rc API is unauthenticated by default and this is a personal machine.
- Health-check via core/version at startup and periodically
- Restart on death, then RECONCILE MOUNTS FROM SCRATCH (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6: 'rclone rcd dies -> detect via health check, restart it, reconcile mounts from scratch'). Restarting without reconciling is worse than not restarting - internal state would describe mounts the new process knows nothing about.
- Stop cleanly at exit; do not orphan the child
- Detect rclone missing from PATH at startup with an actionable message, distinct from 'rclone present but failed to start'

NOTE: rclone is NOT installed on the maintainer's machine (bs-z8u). Everything here must be unit-testable behind an interface with a fake process host. Anything requiring a real rclone binary is a marked Integration test (see tests/Bosun.Tests/TestCategories.cs) and will not run in CI or the default suite.

Acceptance: lifecycle transitions tested against a fake process host - starts, detects death, restarts, gives up gracefully, stops cleanly. Deterministic, injected time.
close_reason: E3 delivered and independently validated: 234/234, 0 warnings, I6/I7 enforcement mutation-tested, no production caller of mount/unmount

title: E3c — Per-host sftp remotes and WinFsp detection
description:
Ensure an sftp remote exists per configured host, derived from hosts.toml via config/create.

- Remote naming must be deterministic and derived from the host's CONFIG KEY, not display_name. E4's IRemoteRootLister takes a hostKey and assumes 'one remote per host, named by key' - confirm that assumption holds here, or reconcile it explicitly and report.
- Map config to sftp remote fields: hostname, port, user, identity_file (key_file). Key-based auth only (ADR-007, Invariant I10) - no password handling.
- Do not clobber unrelated user remotes in rclone.conf. Bosun owns only the remotes it creates; namespace them clearly.
- Recreate/update a remote when the host's config changes.

WINFSP DETECTION at startup (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6): if WinFsp is absent, show an ACTIONABLE message, disable all mount features, and LEAVE TERMINAL FEATURES WORKING. A user without WinFsp should still get their Windows Terminal profiles - degrade, do not fail.

NOTE: WinFsp is NOT installed on the maintainer's machine (bs-z8u), so the detection path is the one that will actually fire on first run. Get its message right; it is the first thing he will see.

Acceptance: remote derivation is a pure, unit-tested mapping from HostConfig to rc parameters. WinFsp detection is behind an injectable probe so both present and absent paths are tested without depending on the machine.
close_reason: E3 delivered and independently validated: 234/234, 0 warnings, I6/I7 enforcement mutation-tested, no production caller of mount/unmount

title: E3b — IRcloneClient: typed wrapper over the rc HTTP API
description:
Thin typed wrapper over the rclone rc HTTP API (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3). HttpClient + System.Text.Json.

Endpoints: core/version, config/create, config/get, mount/mount, mount/unmount, mount/listmounts, operations/list.

INVARIANT I4: every mount operation goes through this HTTP API. NEVER spawn or track `rclone mount` processes. There is exactly one code path for persistent and on-demand tiers; they differ only in who triggers the call.

ARCHITECTURAL BOUNDARY, checked by the validator: this class may EXPOSE mount/mount and mount/unmount, but only IMountSupervisor (E5) may CALL them. Do not call them from anywhere else, and do not add a convenience wrapper that invites it.

INVARIANTS I6 and I7 - enforce at the point mount parameters are built:
  - --vfs-cache-mode is NEVER below `writes`. If config supplies nothing, use `writes`. Config validation rejects off/minimal, but this is a correctness floor and must not depend solely on validation upstream (see bs-mb2, an open decision about exactly where this obligation lives - enforcing it HERE is safe whichever way that goes).
  - --network-mode is ALWAYS passed. Windows optimises fixed and network drives differently; presenting an SFTP mount as a fixed disk produces pathological Explorer behaviour.

rclone rc PARAMETER NAMES ARE A KNOWN TRAP - CLAUDE.md names them as one of two areas where secondhand information is routinely wrong. Verify each endpoint's parameter names against rclone's own current documentation rather than recalling them, and record the source in a comment.

Also implement Bosun.Probe.IRemoteRootLister (defined by E4) using operations/list on the remote root at depth 1. E4 deliberately did not depend on E3; this is where the two meet. Then ADD THE IProbe DI REGISTRATION that E4 left commented out with the exact line to use.

Acceptance: request shaping and response parsing tested against a fake HTTP handler - assert on the actual JSON body sent, especially that vfs cache mode and network mode are present and correct on every mount request. No default-suite test performs real HTTP.
close_reason: E3 delivered and independently validated: 234/234, 0 warnings, I6/I7 enforcement mutation-tested, no production caller of mount/unmount

title: E4c — Backoff ladder with reset triggers
description:
Unreachable -> Probing pacing (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 Backoff).

- Ladder from global.backoff_seconds, default [5, 15, 30, 60, 300], HOLDING at the last value rather than failing or wrapping
- Reset to zero on: network address change, power resume, explicit user retry
- Pure and deterministic: a function of (attempt count, ladder) plus explicit reset. Injected clock, no timers of its own - E5 owns scheduling.

WHY THE RESET MATTERS: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md says this is what makes dock/undock feel immediate rather than sluggish. Without reset, a laptop that failed five times at the office sits at the 300s rung after arriving home and the drive appears minutes late. That is the difference between the tool feeling alive and feeling broken, and it is the acceptance test in docs/OPERATIONS.md T2.

Acceptance: ladder progression asserted rung by rung including the hold-at-last behaviour; each reset trigger tested separately; a ladder of length 1 works; reset mid-ladder returns to the first rung.
close_reason: E4 delivered and independently validated: 187/187, 0 warnings, backoff hold-at-last mutation-tested, shallow/deep result types verified unrelated (I1)

title: E4b — Deep probe seam (operations/list), independent of E3
description:
The deep probe proves authentication and the SFTP subsystem work, by calling operations/list on the remote root at depth 1 (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3).

That is an rclone rc call, which belongs to E3 - but docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md deliberately makes E4 depend only on E2, so E4 must NOT block on E3.

Define the NARROW interface E4 needs (something like IDeepProbeBackend with a single list-root operation), implement IProbe's deep path against it, and provide a fake. E3 will implement that interface with the real rclone rc client. Do not define IRcloneClient here and do not reference rclone types - E3 owns that.

Keep the interface as small as the probe actually needs. A wide interface here becomes a wide fake and a false sense of coverage.

WHY IT MATTERS (Invariant I1): the deep probe runs once before each transition into Mounting, never on the recurring timer. Deep probe FAILURE routes to Draining, never to Mounted. E5 owns that transition, but the probe must give it an unambiguous answer.

Acceptance: deep probe success and failure paths tested against a fake backend; the contract is documented well enough that E3 can implement it without reading E4's internals.
close_reason: E4 delivered and independently validated: 187/187, 0 warnings, backoff hold-at-last mutation-tested, shallow/deep result types verified unrelated (I1)

title: E4a — IProbe contract and shallow TCP probe
description:
The recurring liveness check.

- IProbe contract covering both levels, fakeable (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3)
- Shallow probe: TCP connect to host:port with global.probe_timeout_seconds (default 5), cancellable
- Result model distinguishes success, timeout, refused, DNS failure, and cancelled. E5 logs the trigger for every transition (docs/OPERATIONS.md), so 'why did the probe fail' must survive to the log.
- Injected clock; no real sockets in the default suite

CRITICAL SEMANTICS (Invariant I1): TCP success does NOT imply SFTP success. A shallow probe passing is NEVER sufficient to mount. The type system should make that hard to get wrong - do not let a shallow result be mistaken for a mount authorisation.

Acceptance: shallow probe behaviour is tested against a fake transport - success, timeout, refusal, cancellation - with no real network in the default suite.
close_reason: E4 delivered and independently validated: 187/187, 0 warnings, backoff hold-at-last mutation-tested, shallow/deep result types verified unrelated (I1)

title: needs-decision: what is `<host>` in the ssh commandline E7 emits? (E7/E8 contract)
description:
Raised by the E8 implementer, which could not resolve it and correctly flagged rather than guessing silently. The orchestrator agrees it is unresolved AND thinks the assumption E8 had to make is probably WRONG.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 says a host's Terminal profile commandline is:
    ssh <host>                                  # tmux = false
    ssh -t <host> tmux new -A -s <session>      # tmux = true

It never says what <host> expands to. Two readings, with materially different consequences.

READING A - <host> is the config KEY (what E8 assumed).
Profiles are `ssh example-nas`. This requires the user's own ~/.ssh/config to contain a matching `Host example-nas` block supplying hostname, user, port and identity. Consequences:
  - hostname / port / user / identity_file in hosts.toml would then serve ONLY the rclone sftp remote, never the terminal session. That is coherent but surprising, and nothing documents it.
  - Bosun's Terminal profiles silently depend on an ~/.ssh/config the tool neither reads nor validates. README's Requirements section does not mention needing one. A user who configures hosts.toml correctly and has no ssh config gets profiles that fail to connect, with no diagnostic from Bosun.

READING B - <host> is fully specified from hosts.toml.
Profiles are `ssh -i <identity_file> -p <port> <user>@<hostname>`. Consequences:
  - Profiles work standalone; the four config fields earn their place; nothing depends on external ssh config.
  - E8's SshCommandLineParser BREAKS SILENTLY. It returns null for any token starting with '-', so a fully-specified commandline never correlates. Sessions would show as zero in the tray forever, with no error anywhere - the worst kind of failure, because it looks like "no sessions" rather than "correlation broken".

WHY THE ORCHESTRATOR LEANS B: hosts.toml collects hostname, port, user AND identity_file per host. Under reading A, all four are dead weight for the terminal half of the tool, and Bosun's central selling point (generated Terminal profiles that just work) would rest on configuration Bosun does not own. ADR-010's whole framing is a tool for people with bastion hosts and corporate VPNs; requiring a hand-maintained parallel ~/.ssh/config undercuts that.

BUT reading A is what ARCHITECTURE.md literally shows, and it is genuinely simpler. This needs the maintainer, not a guess.

WHAT TO DO ONCE DECIDED:
  - If A: document the ~/.ssh/config prerequisite in README Requirements and docs/OPERATIONS.md, and add a triage row for "profile opens but connection fails". E8's parser is already correct.
  - If B: E7 emits the full form, AND E8's SshCommandLineParser must be extended to skip flags with values (-i, -p, -o, -l) and to correlate `user@hostname` back to a config key by matching hostname+port+user rather than by key. Add parser fixtures for the exact string E7 emits.

EITHER WAY: E7 and E8 were built independently against the same ambiguous line and MUST be reconciled before E9 renders a session count, or the tray will confidently report zero sessions while sessions are running. Add a test that feeds E7's actual emitted commandline through E8's parser and asserts it correlates - that test is the contract, and it is cheap.

Blocks: correct E7 output, and any trust in E9's session display.
close_reason: ADR-013: commandline uses the config key; ~/.ssh/config prerequisite documented in README and OPERATIONS triage

title: needs-decision: network_mode = false is accepted but Invariant I7 says it must be true
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E2.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's field-semantics table says network_mode "Must be true. Present as a field for debugging only." That sentence appears in the TABLE but NOT in the validation-rules list, and nothing validates it. A user can write network_mode = false today and it passes.

Invariant I7 requires --network-mode on every mount, because Windows optimises fixed and network drives differently and presenting an SFTP mount as a fixed disk produces pathological Explorer behaviour.

"Present for debugging only" reads as "the mounter always passes the flag regardless of this value" - in which case the field is decorative and should be documented as ignored, or removed. But that is an inference, and the ambiguity means the outcome currently depends on E5 code nobody has written.

Options:
  A. Add a validation rule rejecting network_mode = false. Field stays meaningful; user gets a startup error.
  B. Document the field as ignored, always pass --network-mode, and consider deleting it from the schema (ADR-010 warns against settings for options the config already covers).

Recommendation: A. It costs one rule, keeps the field honest, and a user who deliberately sets false is asking for the pathological behaviour and should be told no.

The test-author deliberately wrote no test rather than guess a direction. Decide before E5 consumes this field.
close_reason: Validation-completeness audit: numeric ranges added, vfs_cache_mode converted to a case-insensitive allow-list and defaulted in the config layer, network_mode=false rejected. All rules mutation-verified

title: needs-decision: vfs_cache_mode absent is accepted — where does Invariant I6 actually live?
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E2. Distinct from bs-lrd, which is about UNRECOGNISED values; this is about the field being ABSENT.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's validation rules reject only {off, minimal}. A persistent host that simply omits vfs_cache_mode validates cleanly. Invariant I6 says --vfs-cache-mode writes is "the minimum for EVERY mount".

So I6 currently rests entirely on the mount layer defaulting to `writes` when the field is null. Nothing in the config layer guarantees it, and nothing in the spec says the mount layer must. rclone's own default cache mode is `off`, which is precisely the value I6 forbids - so if E5/E3 simply omit the flag when the config omits the value, we ship the failure I6 exists to prevent, and it presents as "files fail to save from an editor" (docs/OPERATIONS.md triage).

Options:
  A. Make vfs_cache_mode REQUIRED when mode != "none". Config layer guarantees I6; error is locatable at startup.
  B. Keep it optional and write into the spec that IRcloneClient/IMountSupervisor MUST pass --vfs-cache-mode writes when the field is absent. Then E5's brief must carry it.

Either is defensible; what is not defensible is the current state, where the obligation is written in an invariant but implemented nowhere and owned by no component.

Recommendation: B, with the default applied in the CONFIG layer (bind absent -> "writes") so exactly one place decides it and E5 can never see a null. That keeps hosts.toml terse while making the floor structural.

A test documenting the current acceptance already exists (Validate_VfsCacheModeAbsentOnAMountingHost_IsNotAConfigError) so whichever way this goes, the change is deliberate rather than silent drift.
close_reason: Validation-completeness audit: numeric ranges added, vfs_cache_mode converted to a case-insensitive allow-list and defaulted in the config layer, network_mode=false rejected. All rules mutation-verified

title: E8b — ssh.exe enumeration and CIM command-line correlation
description:
Process.GetProcessesByName("ssh") gets the processes; the command line needs CIM (Win32_Process.CommandLine via System.Management or CIM).

- Parse the command line to extract the target host, matching what E7 actually emits: `ssh <host>` and `ssh -t <host> tmux new -A -s <session>`, optionally wrapped in a reconnect loop
- Correlate to the configured host by config key
- Handle the cases that WILL occur: a process that exits between enumeration and query (Win32Exception / ArgumentException), access denied on a process owned by another user, CIM being slow or unavailable
- An ssh.exe the user launched by hand that matches no configured host is not an error - ignore it

Performance matters more than it looks: E9 polls this to render the tray. A CIM query per process on every tick is expensive; measure and consider one query returning all ssh processes.

Acceptance: parsing is a pure, unit-tested function over command-line strings - fixtures covering every form E7 emits plus malformed input. Enumeration itself is behind the interface and not unit-tested against real processes.
close_reason: E8 delivered and independently validated: 158/158, 0 warnings, P/Invoke confined to one file, byte-swap mutation-tested

title: E8a — ISessionMonitor contract, models, and fake
description:
The seam that contains the ugliness.

- ISessionMonitor: enumerate live SSH sessions correlated to configured hosts
- Immutable result model: host key, process id, socket state, remote endpoint, start time
- A fake implementation for tests, and for every other epic that consumes sessions (E9 renders a session count per host)

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3: this is the one component with meaningful P/Invoke; keep it behind the interface and fake it in tests. Correlation is to the CONFIG KEY, not display_name (see bs-08g for why key-vs-display_name identity matters).

Acceptance: the interface and fake exist, are registered in DI, and no consumer needs to know how enumeration works.
close_reason: E8 delivered and independently validated: 158/158, 0 warnings, P/Invoke confined to one file, byte-swap mutation-tested

title: needs-decision: where does an installed Bosun look for hosts.toml?
description:
Raised by the E2 implementer; filed by the orchestrator during validation.

E2 introduced BosunHostOptions.ConfigPath defaulting to <app dir>/config/hosts.toml. That default is an ASSUMPTION, not spec. docs/OPERATIONS.md documents the LOG path (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs\) but is silent on where a deployed Bosun reads its configuration.

This matters because of how Bosun ships: E10 publishes a single-file self-contained EXE, and docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md says config/hosts.toml is gitignored and lives beside the repo. Those two facts do not obviously agree. A single EXE dropped in Downloads with an <app dir>/config/ lookup gives a confusing first run, and a single-file host may resolve <app dir> to an extraction directory rather than where the EXE sits.

Options:
  A. %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\hosts.toml - symmetric with the log path, survives replacing the EXE, standard for per-user config. Requires first-run bootstrap that writes a template from hosts.example.toml.
  B. Beside the executable. Keeps the repo layout, portable/xcopy friendly, but fragile under single-file publish and awkward if the EXE lives in Program Files.
  C. Beside the EXE if present, else %LOCALAPPDATA%. Flexible, but two lookup paths is exactly the kind of thing that produces "why is it reading the wrong config" bug reports.

Recommendation: A, with the current repo-relative path retained ONLY as a dev-time override via BosunHostOptions (which already exists and is injected). Symmetry with the log path is worth a lot for triage - docs/OPERATIONS.md can then say "your config and your logs are both under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun".

RELATED DEFECT, same area: FileSystemConfigWatcher's constructor requires its containing directory to already exist, because System.IO.FileSystemWatcher throws otherwise. First run with no config directory therefore throws before any friendly "no configuration found" message can be produced. Whatever path is chosen, first-run bootstrap needs to handle a missing directory gracefully. E10's brief already lists "detect missing WinFsp / rclone / config, guide to setup" - this is that work, discovered early.

BLOCKS a correct E10 first-run experience. Does not block E3/E4/E5, which take config through the injected option.
notes: Folded into ADR-012 (PROPOSED): recommendation is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\hosts.toml for symmetry with the log path, with the repo-relative path surviving only as a dev override.
close_reason: E12b/E12c delivered and validated: 407/407, ordering and gate both mutation-verified, Independent suite untouched

title: needs-decision: profile identity vs host renames (E7)
description:
Surfaced by verified research into Terminal's fragment GUID derivation (see bs-3ir design notes).

Terminal derives a fragment profile's GUID as UUIDv5(UUIDv5(TERMINAL_FRAGMENT_NS, app-name), profile-name). The GUID is therefore a hash of the profile NAME.

Consequence: if a host's profile name changes in config/hosts.toml, the derived GUID changes, and Terminal treats it as an entirely new profile. Any customisation the user layered onto the old profile in their own settings.json (keyed by the old GUID) is silently orphaned, and the renamed host appears fresh and uncustomised.

This mechanism is directly documented. The user-facing consequence is inferred from it (high confidence mechanically, but not spelled out by Microsoft as a warning).

Options:
  A. Treat host profile names as immutable identity once created. Simplest; costs the user the ability to rename a host without losing Terminal-side customisation. Document it.
  B. Emit an explicit stable `guid` derived by Bosun from the host's config KEY (e.g. `hosts.example-nas`) rather than its display_name. Renames of display_name then preserve identity. Costs us owning the GUID derivation and a migration story for anyone who already has profiles.
  C. Do nothing and accept silent orphaning on rename.

Recommendation: B. The config key is already the stable identifier everywhere else in the system, display_name is explicitly a presentation field, and B costs one UUIDv5 implementation we can verify against Microsoft's own published test vector (app "Git", profile "Git Bash" -> {2ece5bfe-50ed-5f3a-ab87-5cd4baafed2b}).

BLOCKS E7 implementation. Do not guess - this is an identity contract that is painful to change after users have profiles.
close_reason: ADR-013: Bosun emits an explicit guid derived from the config key, so renaming display_name no longer orphans customisation

title: E1c — Serilog rolling-file logging
description:
Serilog wired into the Generic Host.

- Rolling daily file under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs\ plus a debug sink
- Structured output; the log path must be injectable so tests never write to the real %LOCALAPPDATA% location
- Integrated via Microsoft.Extensions.Logging so ILogger<T> injection works throughout

Why it matters: docs/OPERATIONS.md makes the log the primary triage artifact — every state transition will be logged with host, from-state, to-state, and trigger (E5). Get the shape right now so E5 can just use it.

Acceptance: a test writes to a temp log path and asserts the file is produced and parseable; no test writes to the real %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs\.
close_reason: E1 delivered and independently validated: 0 warnings, 5/5 tests, mutation-tested, real %LOCALAPPDATA% untouched

title: E7 — Windows Terminal fragment writer
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E7. Spec: ADR-006.

- Verify the current fragment directory for Store vs unpackaged Terminal against Microsoft documentation before implementing — do not hardcode from memory
- Serialise host list to fragment schema: name, commandline, colour scheme, tab colour, icon
- tmux variant: ssh -t <host> tmux new -A -s <session>
- Optional reconnect wrapper script generation (retry on exit 255, exit cleanly on 0)
- Rewrite on config change; never touch settings.json
- Test: fragment is valid JSON, Terminal loads it, wt -w 0 new-tab -p "<host>" opens a session

Invariant I5. Tests write to a temp directory injected via the interface, never the real Fragments\Bosun\ path.

Good first task for the researcher subagent: the fragment directory and schema are an area where secondhand information is routinely wrong.
design:
VERIFIED against Microsoft Learn (ms.date 2025-11-10, fetched 2026-08-16), per ADR-006's instruction to verify rather than hardcode.

FRAGMENT PATH (high confidence)
Two supported locations, both read regardless of whether Terminal itself is Store or unpackaged:
  all-users:  C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\{app}\{file}.json
  per-user:   %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\{app}\{file}.json
Bosun is an unpackaged per-user win-x64 EXE, so use the per-user path:
  %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\bosun.json
NOTE the "Microsoft\" path segment - ADR-006 and CLAUDE.md I5 both abbreviate this as
"...\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\" and omit it. The Store-vs-unpackaged distinction in
ADR-006's note is a red herring: it applies only to Store-PACKAGED APPS registering via an
app-extension manifest (PublicFolder\Fragments), which is a different mechanism Bosun does not use.
Terminal Preview: docs do not state a separate Fragments dir; this sub-point is inferred, not sourced.

SCHEMA (high confidence)
Top level: two optional arrays, "profiles" and "schemes".
Profile entries are either new profiles (name REQUIRED) or {"updates": "{guid}", ...overrides}.
Fragments accept the full standard profile object - name, commandline, startingDirectory, icon,
colorScheme, tabColor all supported.
icon: relative paths resolve against the fragment dir only on Terminal >= 1.24; web URLs otherwise.
startingDirectory: the docs self-contradict on the default (states %USERPROFILE%, then lists four
launch-context-dependent defaults). SET IT EXPLICITLY per host rather than relying on any default.
Fragment "schemes" entries must define name plus ALL 16 colour-table entries; partial schemes rejected.

PROFILE GUID (high confidence - refines ADR-006's wording)
UUIDv5, two-level derivation:
  appNamespace = UUIDv5(TERMINAL_FRAGMENT_NS, app-name), TERMINAL_FRAGMENT_NS = {f65ddb7e-706b-4499-8a50-40313caf510a}
  profileGuid  = UUIDv5(appNamespace, profile-name)
Name strings encoded UTF-16LE before hashing.
Documented test vector: app "Git", profile "Git Bash" -> {2ece5bfe-50ed-5f3a-ab87-5cd4baafed2b}.
USE THAT AS A UNIT TEST. If our derivation reproduces it, the implementation is right.
Emitting "guid" ourselves is optional but "strongly encouraged" by the docs. Recommended: omit it and
let Terminal derive, treating (app-name, profile-name) as the identity contract - but see bs- issue on
renames before committing to that.

COLOUR SCHEME SCOPE (medium-high confidence)
Scheme names live in one global namespace merged from the user's settings.json and all fragments.
A fragment profile may reference a scheme the user defined. Collision behaviour for duplicate scheme
names is NOT documented anywhere on Learn - a real documentation gap.

FAILURE MODES (medium confidence - sourced from the Terminal repo, not Learn; Learn is silent)
Since microsoft/terminal#10601 (fixes #10590, shipped 1.10.1933.0), Terminal wraps per-fragment parsing
in try/catch: a malformed fragment is skipped and other fragments still load. Before that, one bad
fragment broke all of them.
There is NO UI surface, toast, or default log indicating a fragment failed to load. So: validate our
own JSON before writing it, and treat "profiles appear in Terminal's dropdown" as the only available
confirmation. docs/OPERATIONS.md "Terminal profiles missing" triage should say this.
microsoft/terminal#13916: removing a profile reference from a fragment does not always take effect
cleanly - relevant when a host is deleted from hosts.toml.

wt.exe (high confidence)
`wt -w 0 new-tab -p "<profile name>"` is current. -w 0 is documented as "most recently used window".
-p takes the profile NAME; quote names containing spaces.
Duplicate/ambiguous profile names: undocumented tie-breaking, and an unrecognised name appears to fall
back silently rather than error (microsoft/terminal#6086). ALREADY MITIGATED: docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md
validation already rejects duplicate display_name, so E2 enforces the uniqueness E7 depends on.
Cross-check that rule survives E2 implementation.

title: E3 — rclone rc client and rcd process lifecycle
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E3. Spec: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.

- RcloneProcessService: start rclone rcd on a configurable loopback port, health-check via core/version, restart on death, stop cleanly on exit
- IRcloneClient typed wrapper: config/create, config/get, mount/mount, mount/unmount, mount/listmounts, operations/list
- Ensure an sftp remote exists per configured host, derived from config
- WinFsp presence detection at startup with an actionable message
- Integration tests against a real rclone rcd where feasible; otherwise a fake

Invariant I4: all mount operations go through the rc HTTP API, never by spawning rclone mount. Only IMountSupervisor may call mount/mount and mount/unmount — IRcloneClient exposes them, nothing else invokes them.

Anything touching a real rclone rcd or WinFsp is a MARKED INTEGRATION TEST excluded from the default suite.
close_reason: All three E3 children delivered and validated; E4 seam (IRemoteRootLister, IProbe DI) closed

title: E8 — Session monitor: ssh.exe enumeration and TCP state
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E8. Spec: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 (ISessionMonitor).

- Enumerate ssh.exe via Process.GetProcessesByName
- Resolve command lines via CIM to correlate process → configured host
- GetExtendedTcpTable P/Invoke for socket state
- All of it behind ISessionMonitor, faked in tests
- Isolated in one file; this is the ugliest code in the project

P/Invoke must not leak beyond the ISessionMonitor implementation — the validator checks this explicitly. If interop starts appearing in a second file, stop and escalate.
close_reason: All three E8 children delivered and validated

title: E4 — Probe engine: shallow, deep, backoff ladder
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E4. Spec: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 (IProbe) and §4.

- Shallow probe: TCP connect with timeout
- Deep probe: operations/list root, depth 1 — proves auth and SFTP subsystem
- Backoff ladder with reset triggers (network change, resume, manual retry)
- IProbe fakeable for tests

TCP success does not imply SFTP success — never mount on a shallow probe alone (Invariant I1). Probe scheduling is state-dependent, not purely config-driven: see ADR-011 and bs child issue on mounted-host probing.
close_reason: All three E4 children delivered and validated

title: E6 — System event integration: power, network, session
description:
Seeded from docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E6. Spec: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 (ISystemEventSource).

- PowerModeChanged Suspend → unmount all, bounded time budget (suspend_unmount_timeout_seconds, default 8s — Windows will not wait forever)
- PowerModeChanged Resume → re-probe all, bypass backoff
- NetworkAddressChanged → reset backoff, force-probe mounted hosts
- Test with real sleep/resume and a real network change; manual protocol in docs/OPERATIONS.md T1/T2

Invariant I8. docs/OPERATIONS.md T2 (close lid on LAN, open on another network, nothing wedged) is the acceptance test that matters for v1.

Send test-author independently (CLAUDE.md §6).

title: Validate mounted_probe_interval_seconds and probe intervals (ADR-011)
description:
Config-layer half of ADR-011.

- Bind new global setting mounted_probe_interval_seconds. Default 60 when absent.
- Reject the whole config if probe.interval_seconds is negative.
- Reject the whole config if mounted_probe_interval_seconds is zero or negative. ABSENT IS NOT AN ERROR - it defaults to 60, consistent with every other [global] field. Rejecting a config for a newly-introduced key would break every existing hosts.toml on upgrade.
- Rejection semantics are unchanged: whole config refused, previous config retained, error surfaced.

Spec: docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md (global block, field semantics table, validation rules) and ADR-011.

Acceptance criteria:
- A config omitting mounted_probe_interval_seconds parses and yields 60.
- mounted_probe_interval_seconds = 0 is rejected; the previous config is retained.
- mounted_probe_interval_seconds negative is rejected.
- probe.interval_seconds negative is rejected.
- probe.interval_seconds = 0 parses (it is the documented on-demand default).
- One test per rule, each failing for one describable reason.

title: Install WinFsp and rclone on the dev machine
description:
Neither WinFsp nor rclone is currently installed on the maintainer's machine (verified: `rclone` not on PATH, C:\Program Files (x86)\WinFsp absent). dotnet 10.0.302, Windows Terminal, uv, bd and graphify are all present.

rclone v1.75.0 INSTALLED 2026-08-16, user-scope at %LOCALAPPDATA%\rclone, added to the USER PATH
(not machine - no admin, trivially reversible). Installed by direct download rather than winget,
