title: Add OPERATIONS.md T-row for the deep-probe-detects-dead-mount scenario (ADR-016)
description: bs-2eg / ADR-016 added a periodic deep probe for Mounted hosts (global.mounted_deep_probe_interval_seconds, default 300s, fixed 2-failure threshold) to detect a dead SSH channel underneath a mount that a shallow TCP probe cannot see (sleep/resume, a short network blip). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/DECISIONS.md (ADR-016) now document the mechanism and its worst-case detection latency (2 x mounted_deep_probe_interval_seconds, default 600s/10min), but docs/OPERATIONS.md's manual test protocol (T1-T3) was not updated with a scenario for it -- T3 only covers the existing shallow-probe-driven unmount-on-failure case. Add a T-row exercising: mount a host, kill the SSH session under it while keeping TCP port 22 reachable (e.g. restart sshd without dropping the port, or a firewall rule that RSTs new connections but the existing rclone session degrades), and confirm the drive disappears within the documented worst case rather than wedging Explorer. Likely folds into bs-aya / bs-xd6 (rewriting the manual protocol around real hardware) rather than being done standalone -- check dependency before starting.

title: Amend ADR-001: the laptop justification does not match the deployment
description:
ADR-001 chose .NET over Python primarily on system-event integration, and justified it: "For a laptop tool used many hours a day, closing the lid at one location and opening it at another is the central use case, not an edge case."

The maintainer runs a Windows DESKTOP; his laptop is a Mac, which cannot run Bosun at all. So the central use case named in the ADR does not exist for the only user.

DO NOT REVERSE THE DECISION. .NET still looks right on the other three grounds ADR-001 gives - hosting model, single-file packaging, and keeping an Explorer shell extension reachable - and the system-event integration is still needed, just for different events: sleep and wake on a desktop, and network interruption, rather than dock and undock.

What needs correcting is the REASONING, because ADR-001's opening line is what the rest of the project's emphasis was built on. Everything downstream - the weight given to suspend/resume, T2 being the acceptance test, the README's "closing the lid at the office and opening it at home" - inherits a premise that is not true of the deployment.

Amend with: what the real scenarios are, that the events still matter (a desktop sleeps, and a network still drops), and that the decision stands on its remaining grounds. Also fix README's laptop framing, which is user-facing and simply describes someone else's machine.

Worth recording honestly that this was caught late - the assumption was inherited from the spec and repeated back many times without ever being checked against the machine the code was being built on.

title: E6c — Make the manual protocol runnable and record what T1-T3 actually did
description:
docs/OPERATIONS.md's manual protocol has never been run, because until now there was nothing to run it against. Both prerequisites are installed and a real SFTP mount has been proven end to end, so T1-T4 and T6 become executable once E6 lands.

This issue is the doc half, done AFTER E6a/E6b:
  - Update the protocol with the concrete commands the maintainer will actually type, now that they are known - the rc port, how to see current mounts, where the transition log is.
  - Add a row for reading the supervisor's transition log, since that is the artifact that explains a T3 result.
  - Record the result of the first real run: what happened, what the log said, what was surprising.

T2 is the one that matters (close the lid on the LAN, open on another network, nothing wedged). traininggrounds at 192.168.0.144 is a LAN host, which makes it the natural T2 subject: mounted at home, lid closed, opened elsewhere, the drive must be GONE rather than wedged, and must return on coming back.

Do not fabricate results. Write the protocol; leave the results section explicitly empty until a run actually happens.
notes: SUPERSEDED IN PART by the new protocol-rewrite issue: this issue assumed the laptop dock/undock scenario, which does not apply - the maintainer has a Windows desktop and a Mac laptop, so T2 as written cannot be run at all. The real scenarios are overnight sleep and network interruption.

title: rclone is not on PATH for already-running shells — RcloneProcessService should fall back to a known install location
description:
Noticed while running the real-binary integration tests.

rclone was installed to %LOCALAPPDATA%\rclone and added to the USER PATH, but shells started BEFORE that change do not see it: `where rclone` fails in this session even though %LOCALAPPDATA%\rclone\rclone.exe runs fine when invoked directly. That is ordinary Windows PATH-propagation behaviour, not a bug.

But it is a first-run experience problem for Bosun. A user who installs rclone and then starts Bosun from an existing Explorer session - or has Bosun already running at login - gets RcloneExecutableNotFoundException even though rclone is installed. The error message would say rclone is missing, and the user would reasonably disagree.

Options:
  A. Resolve rclone by searching PATH, then falling back to known install locations (%LOCALAPPDATA%\rclone, %ProgramFiles%\rclone, winget's package path) before declaring it missing.
  B. Make the not-found message say where Bosun looked and suggest restarting Bosun after installing.
  C. Add an explicit rclone_path setting to [global].

Recommend A plus B: search the obvious places, and when it genuinely is not there, say what was searched. C is worth having as an escape hatch but should not be required for the common case.

Relates to ADR-012's degradation model: rclone missing is one of the documented degraded states, so the message it produces is part of the contract.

title: ConfigValidator does not enforce tmux = true implies tmux_session
description:
Found by the E7 implementer. A gap in E2, surfaced by E7 needing the value.

session.tmux = true with no session.tmux_session passes validation. FragmentProfileGenerator defends by falling back to "main" rather than throwing, which is reasonable defence-in-depth but means a user who forgot the field silently gets a session named "main" rather than being told.

This is exactly the class the validation-completeness audit (bs-z3y) was about: the spec implies an obligation - tmux_session is only meaningful when tmux is true, and is required then - and validation does not enforce it. The audit covered [global] numerics and the invariant-bearing mount fields; this is a per-host conditional requirement it did not reach.

Fix: reject tmux = true with a null or empty tmux_session, and add the rule to docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's validation list. Keep the generator's fallback as defence-in-depth with a comment saying validation should have caught it, matching the pattern already used for failures_before_unmount and vfs_cache_mode.

While there: the audit's stated PRINCIPLE was about [global] values feeding safety decisions. Worth extending the wording to cover per-host conditional requirements too, since that is what this is.
close_reason: Fragment writer wired early and ungated; tmux_session validation added; reconnect loop capped. All mutation-verified; the errorlevel diagnosis was corrected and independently confirmed (9009 vs >= semantics)

title: E7d — Amend ADR-006 and Invariant I5 with the verified path and GUID algorithm
description:
Supersedes bs-7e8. Do this once E7a-E7c prove the path works, not before - the spec should record what shipped.

1. PATH. ADR-006 and CLAUDE.md Invariant I5 both write the location as "...\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\", omitting the `Microsoft\` segment. Correct both to the verified full path.

2. THE STORE-VS-UNPACKAGED NOTE IS WRONG. ADR-006 says "The fragment directory differs between Store and unpackaged Terminal installs." Verified: it does not. Replace it with the verified fact so nobody re-litigates it.

3. GUID WORDING. ADR-006 says fragments "yield stable profile GUIDs derived from source name plus profile name" - directionally right, mechanically vague. Record the UUIDv5 two-level derivation and the published test vector.

CAUTION: CLAUDE.md §2 is mirrored into the five .claude/agents/*.md definitions, which carry their own copies of the load-bearing rules. If I5's text changes, check whether the agent definitions quote the path and keep them in sync - CLAUDE.md §6 says both are reviewed artifacts. I5's SUBSTANCE (never touch settings.json) is correct and must not change; only the path text.

title: Stale WinFsp uninstall entry with no actual WinFsp — real-world detector edge case
description:
Found on the maintainer's own machine while attempting the WinFsp install (2026-08-16).

Add/Remove Programs lists: "WinFsp installed by Bitvise SSH Client (remove only)" - an orphaned uninstall stub, presumably left by the Bitvise install that ADR-007 describes Bosun as replacing.

But WinFsp is NOT functionally present:
  * no C:\Program Files (x86)\WinFsp directory
  * no HKLM\SOFTWARE\WinFsp and no HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp key
  * no WinFsp driver service

WHY THIS VALIDATES A DESIGN CHOICE: a detector that checked Add/Remove Programs - a very natural implementation, and the first thing many people would reach for - would report WinFsp PRESENT and be wrong. Every mount would then fail with a confusing rclone error instead of Bosun's actionable 'WinFsp is not installed' message. That is the worst possible first-run outcome: the tool says everything is fine and nothing works.

E3's WinFspDetector reads HKLM\SOFTWARE\WinFsp\InstallDir via the 32-bit registry view and correctly reports ABSENT. So the approach is right, and it is now validated against a real machine rather than assumed.

WORK: add a test documenting this case so nobody later 'improves' the detector by switching it to an uninstall-registry scan. The fake-based test should assert that presence is determined by InstallDir and by nothing else, with a comment naming the Bitvise stub as the reason.

ALSO CHECK once WinFsp is actually installed: that the stale Bitvise entry does not confuse the real installer or leave two competing entries.

title: Assert mounted drive is DriveType.Network after every mount (I7 runtime guard)
description:
From the bs-1sy recommendation, approved 2026-08-16. Independent of whether the manual network_mode experiment succeeds - do this regardless.

After a successful mount, read new DriveInfo(<letter>).DriveType and surface an error if it is Fixed rather than Network.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE MANUAL CHECK: bs-1sy establishes whether rclone honours network_mode as a flat rc parameter TODAY. This assertion establishes it FOREVER - including after an rclone upgrade renames or removes the parameter. If the name is wrong rclone very likely IGNORES the unknown key rather than erroring, the mount succeeds, and it presents as a fixed disk. That is exactly the pathological-Explorer condition I7 exists to prevent, and no unit test can catch it: the existing assertion that network_mode is in the JSON body passes whether or not rclone understands it.

Pure BCL - DriveInfo.DriveType needs no P/Invoke, so it raises no question about interop confinement (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 keeps P/Invoke behind ISessionMonitor; this is not P/Invoke).

Belongs with IMountSupervisor's post-mount path, since that is where a mount is confirmed. Surface a failure the same way other degradations surface per ADR-012 - this is a condition the user needs to see, not a log line.

Acceptance: a fake reporting Fixed causes the mount to be treated as failed/surfaced; a fake reporting Network passes. The real DriveInfo read is behind an injected seam so no default-suite test touches a real drive letter.
notes:
PREMISE FALSIFIED - verified against real rclone v1.75.0, and this downgrades the issue.

This issue was filed on my own strongly-argued claim that "if the name is wrong rclone very likely
IGNORES the unknown key rather than erroring, the mount succeeds, and it presents as a fixed disk."
That claim is WRONG.

Tested directly: mount/mount with a deliberately misspelled `netwrok_mode` returns
500 Internal Server Error and NO MOUNT IS CREATED (DriveType = NoRootDirectory). rclone validates
its rc parameter names and rejects unknown ones loudly.

So the specific catastrophic scenario this guard was designed for - a silently-ignored parameter
producing a fixed-disk mount that looks fine and wedges Explorer - DOES NOT EXIST for a parameter
rename. A future rclone that renames or drops network_mode would break the mount immediately and
visibly, which is the good failure mode.

WHAT REMAINS, and why this is not simply closed:
  - rclone could keep the NAME and change the SEMANTICS (accept network_mode and stop acting on it).
    A name check cannot catch that; a DriveType check can.
  - The assertion is nearly free: new DriveInfo(letter).DriveType, pure BCL, no P/Invoke.
  - It converts an I7 violation from "invisible" to "reported" for any cause, not just renames.

RECOMMENDATION: implement it, but as ordinary defence-in-depth at P2 rather than the P0 this was
filed as. The urgency came from a premise that turned out to be false, and the honest thing is to
say so rather than let the priority stand on a dead argument.

VERIFIED BASELINE for the assertion: a correct mount of an sftp remote with network_mode=true gives
DriveType=Network, DriveFormat=FUSE-rclone.

title: Re-export .beads/issues.jsonl after merges instead of resolving conflicts by hand
description:
The bulk merge of the stacked PR chain conflicted on .beads/issues.jsonl in three PRs (#2, #4, #6), which closed them and broke the path to main.

Root cause: .beads/issues.jsonl is a GENERATED export committed to git. Every branch regenerated it, so every branch diverged, and pairwise merges against moving bases conflicted on a file nobody edits by hand.

The Dolt database is the source of truth; the JSONL is a projection of it. So a conflict in the export is never a real conflict - the resolution is always 'run bd export again'.

Options:
  A. A .gitattributes entry giving .beads/issues.jsonl a custom merge driver that just re-runs bd export. Correct, and invisible once set up.
  B. Convention: on any conflict in that file, take either side and immediately re-export. Zero setup, relies on remembering.
  C. Stop committing the export and rely on Dolt remotes for sharing. Contradicts the intent recorded in the root .gitignore and CLAUDE.md §3, which want the issue graph to survive a clone.

Recommend A, falling back to B. Do not do C without revisiting CLAUDE.md §3.

Note for future stacked work: the deeper lesson is that a long stack multiplies this - nine branches each carrying a generated file guarantees conflicts. Shorter chains, or merging more often, would have avoided it independently of the file itself.
close_reason: Resolved structurally: interactions.jsonl gitignored (audit trail, no clone value); issues.jsonl stays committed with a documented re-export resolution in .gitignore and CLAUDE.md §3

title: RATIFY: is 8s the right suspend budget? (mechanism bug fixed in PR #8)
description:
Found by INDEPENDENT adversarial testing of E5.

Forced-unmount escalation is evaluated only on a drain RETRY tick, and DrainRetryInterval is 5s. So the 8s suspend budget (global.suspend_unmount_timeout_seconds) and the 10s ordinary drain timeout BOTH escalate at t=10. The suspend budget has no observable effect unless it is set below 5s.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 says the suspend handler 'must complete quickly. Windows does not wait indefinitely. Issue unmounts with a short timeout and accept that a forced unmount may be needed on resume.' In practice Windows allows roughly two seconds. A forced unmount landing at t=10 arrives long after the machine has already gone to sleep, so the escalation that Invariant I8 depends on never actually happens during suspend.

Consequence: mounts survive suspend more often than the design intends, and the machine wakes with drive letters pointing at whatever network it is now on - the exact condition docs/OPERATIONS.md T2 (the acceptance test that matters) exists to prevent. Resume-side reconciliation should still recover it, but I8's whole point is to unmount BEFORE sleeping rather than relying on cleanup afterwards.

FIX: the suspend budget must bound the escalation deadline directly rather than being rounded up to retry granularity. Fix in progress.

Worth deciding alongside: is 8s even the right default, given the real Windows window is nearer 2s? That is a config default question for the maintainer, separate from the mechanism bug.
notes: MECHANISM FIX LANDED in PR #8 - the suspend budget now bounds the escalation deadline directly instead of rounding up to the 5s retry grid. What remains is a defaults question: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 says Windows does not wait indefinitely, and the real window is nearer 2s than 8s. Is suspend_unmount_timeout_seconds = 8 still right?

title: Supervisor does not react to config changes; no SupervisorService BackgroundService wrapper
description:
Two related gaps the E5 implementer flagged rather than quietly leaving.

1. MountSupervisor builds its host set once at StartAsync and does not subscribe to IHostConfigStore.ConfigChanged. Adding, removing, or reconfiguring a host therefore requires restarting the app - even though E2 built the whole watch-and-reload machinery specifically so it would not.

The interesting part is not the subscription, it is the semantics. When a host's config changes while it is Mounted, what happens? A changed drive letter or remote_path means the live mount no longer matches intent, so it presumably must drain and remount. A changed tab_color means nothing to the supervisor at all. Blindly re-arming every host on any config change would unmount drives because the user edited a colour - which is an unmount the user did not ask for, and the tool's whole promise is that drives disappear only for good reason.

So this needs a diff: which config fields are mount-relevant, and only those trigger a re-arm.

2. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2 lists SupervisorService : BackgroundService in the process model. It does not exist. MountSupervisor.RunAsync is the loop such a wrapper would call; the state-machine logic it runs is well tested, but the wrapper itself is not written. Fold into the composition-root work alongside bs-127 and bs-p1.

3. Also noted, lower stakes: GetSnapshot() reads mutable HostRuntime fields without locking against the channel loop. Fine in practice for a UI snapshot of simple fields, but not formally race-free under TimeProvider.System. Worth revisiting when E9 actually consumes it at a UI refresh rate.

4. Idle-unmount (rule 7) has no filesystem-activity signal wired anywhere yet. RecordActivityAsync is the seam and is currently uncalled, so idle-unmount cannot fire in practice. Needs a source - rclone rc core/stats or vfs stats are the plausible candidates - and that is real work, not a wiring detail.

title: needs-decision: is `Probing` a one-shot state, or does every recurring probe re-enter it?
description:
Surfaced by the E5 implementer as an inference it made but could not confirm from the spec.

It read docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 as: Probing is a ONE-SHOT state, entered only from Disabled (the initial check). Recurring idle and mounted probes then happen 'in place' in Ready / Unreachable / Mounted without re-entering Probing.

That reading matches IProbe's own doc comment verbatim, and it makes the diagram's arrows work. But §4 never says it, and the diagram can equally be read as every probe cycling back through Probing.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: docs/OPERATIONS.md makes the transition log the primary triage artifact, and every transition is logged with from-state, to-state and trigger. If recurring probes re-entered Probing, the log would record a transition per probe per host - on a 60s cadence with several hosts that is a lot of noise, and it would bury the transitions that actually matter. The one-shot reading produces a log where a state change means something happened.

So the implementer's reading is very likely correct AND better. It just is not written down, which means the next person to touch the state machine can reasonably conclude the opposite.

Action: state it explicitly in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 - either as a note on the diagram or as an eighth transition rule. Cheap, and it closes a real ambiguity in the project's most important spec section.

title: Establish a marked-integration-test convention for real interop and rclone
description:
Raised by the E8 implementer. Every epic from here on needs this and none has it yet.

CLAUDE.md and the agent definitions repeatedly require that anything touching real WinFsp, a real rclone rcd, a real drive letter, real processes or the real Windows Terminal fragment path be a MARKED INTEGRATION TEST excluded from the default suite and run deliberately by the human. That rule has been honoured so far by simply not writing such tests at all.

That is fine up to E8 but stops working at E3 (rclone rc client), E6 (real suspend/resume) and E10 (packaging), where the only meaningful verification IS against real components.

Needed:
  - A convention, e.g. [Trait("Category","Integration")], and the exact dotnet test filter that excludes it (--filter "Category!=Integration")
  - .github/workflows/build.yml updated to use that filter, so CI never attempts a real mount on a GitHub runner
  - A documented command in docs/OPERATIONS.md for running integration tests deliberately on the maintainer's machine
  - Retrofit the currently-unwritten cases: real Win32TcpConnectionReader.GetConnections(), real CimSshProcessEnumerator.Enumerate()

Do this BEFORE E3, so the rclone client's integration tests are born in the right shape rather than retrofitted. Cheap now, annoying later.

Note the safety stake: a default-suite test that reaches a real IRcloneClient can mount a drive on the maintainer's machine. The convention is what makes that structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.
close_reason: Convention established and verified empirically: safe-by-default via runsettings, opt-in via --settings, canary test proves the exclusion works

title: needs-decision: are [session] and [probe] fields required, or defaulted?
description:
Found by independent adversarial testing of E2.

The E2 parser requires autostart, reconnect, tmux, tab_color, color_scheme, interval_seconds and deep_probe to be present, and throws a PARSE error otherwise. docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md shows them all in its example but never says they are required and gives no defaults.

So a user writing a minimal host block gets a hard parse failure on a key they had no way to know was mandatory. For a tool whose config is hand-edited, that is a poor first experience, and it is the kind of friction that generates the bug reports CONTRIBUTING.md invites.

tab_color and color_scheme in particular look like natural defaults - a host with no colour preference is a completely reasonable thing to write, and E7 can emit a profile without either.

Options:
  A. Document them as required in docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md. Cheapest; keeps the model strict.
  B. Give documented defaults (tmux=false, reconnect=true, autostart=false, deep_probe=true, interval_seconds=0, tab_color/color_scheme absent -> Terminal's own default) and make them optional.

Recommendation: B for the [session] block, A for [probe]. Probe cadence genuinely affects safety (see the ADR-011 class of bug) and should be a conscious choice per host; colours should not be.

Related to bs-o09 (first-run experience).

title: E8c — GetExtendedTcpTable P/Invoke for socket state
description:
Socket state per ssh.exe process, via GetExtendedTcpTable (iphlpapi.dll) with TCP_TABLE_OWNER_PID_ALL.

- The two-call buffer-sizing dance: call once with a null buffer to learn the required size, allocate, call again. The size can change between calls, so loop rather than assuming the second call succeeds.
- Marshal MIB_TCPROW_OWNER_PID rows; ports are big-endian in the struct and need byte-swapping - a classic source of nonsense port numbers
- Map owning PID to the ssh.exe processes found in E8b, exposing connection state (ESTABLISHED, SYN_SENT, etc.)
- Free/allocate correctly; this runs on E9's polling interval, so a leak here compounds

ALL P/Invoke stays in this one file. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3 and the validator both check that interop does not spread beyond the ISessionMonitor implementation - if you find yourself adding a DllImport to a second file, stop and report.

Acceptance: struct layout and the port byte-swap are unit-tested against known byte patterns without calling the real API. The real call is exercised only in a marked integration test the human runs deliberately.
close_reason: E8 delivered and independently validated: 158/158, 0 warnings, P/Invoke confined to one file, byte-swap mutation-tested

title: needs-decision: should vfs_cache_mode use an allow-list rather than a deny-list?
description:
Raised by the E2 implementer; filed by the orchestrator during validation.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's validation rules say to reject vfs_cache_mode in {off, minimal}. E2 implemented that literally - a DENY-list. Consequence: a typo such as "wirtes" or "Writes" passes config validation and is only rejected later by rclone at mount time, if at all.

Why this is more than tidiness. Invariant I6 says --vfs-cache-mode writes is the MINIMUM for every mount, and the stated reason is that anything less makes editors and Office fail to save files. A value rclone does not recognise could be silently ignored or defaulted by rclone, which would land us below the floor without any error - the failure would appear as "files fail to save from an editor", which docs/OPERATIONS.md's triage table attributes to exactly this cause. Validation is supposed to be what catches that.

Options:
  A. Allow-list {writes, full}. These are the only two values docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md permits ("writes is the floor... full also permitted"). Anything else is rejected with a locatable error. Strictest, and matches I6's intent rather than its literal wording.
  B. Keep the deny-list as specified. Literal compliance with the written rule; leaves the typo hole open.

Recommendation: A. The schema already enumerates exactly two acceptable values, so an allow-list encodes the same intent with no loss of capability, and it converts a silent runtime failure into a startup error the user can act on. If rclone later gains a mode we want, adding it to the list is a one-line change with a doc update - which is the correct amount of friction for something governed by an invariant.

If A is accepted, docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's rule text should change from the deny-list phrasing to the allow-list phrasing so spec and code agree.
notes: ADDITIONAL, from independent adversarial testing: the deny-list is ORDINAL/case-sensitive, so "Off", "OFF" and "MINIMAL" pass validation today. If rclone parses its cache-mode flag case-insensitively (NOT verified - do not assume), that is a live Invariant I6 bypass rather than a typo problem: it is the exact value the spec rejects, spelled differently. Fold into this decision - if the answer is an allow-list, make it case-insensitive, or reject anything not already lowercase.
close_reason: Validation-completeness audit: numeric ranges added, vfs_cache_mode converted to a case-insensitive allow-list and defaulted in the config layer, network_mode=false rejected. All rules mutation-verified

title: vfs_cache_mode has no exhaustive allow-list in validation
description: docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md's validation rules only reject mount.vfs_cache_mode when it is exactly 'off' or 'minimal'; anything else -- including a typo like 'wrties' or a value rclone doesn't recognize -- passes ConfigValidator silently and would only fail much later at rclone rc mount time. Implemented bs-c0g literally per the documented rule list (reject-set membership only), but flagging as a possible schema gap: worth deciding whether to add a positive allow-list ({writes, full}) instead of/in addition to the reject-list.

title: Confirm real hosts.toml location convention for installed Bosun
description: bs-30b wires IHostConfigStore into BosunHostFactory DI via BosunHostOptions.ConfigPath. CreateDefault() currently assumes <app directory>/config/hosts.toml (mirroring this repo's own layout), but docs/OPERATIONS.md does not state where an installed, packaged copy of Bosun should look for its config -- it only documents %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\logs for logs. Confirm the intended convention (next to the exe vs %LOCALAPPDATA%\Bosun\ vs something else) and update BosunHostOptions.CreateDefault() + docs/OPERATIONS.md to match. Also note: FileSystemConfigWatcher's constructor requires its containing directory to already exist (System.IO.FileSystemWatcher throws otherwise), so first-run bootstrapping needs to ensure the config directory exists (or produce an actionable 'no config found' error) before DI resolves IHostConfigStore -- currently unhandled.

title: needs-decision: should Bosun survive a DispatcherUnhandledException? (E9)
description:
Raised by the E1 implementer and deliberately not guessed at.

src/Bosun/App.xaml.cs OnDispatcherUnhandledException currently LOGS ONLY and does not set e.Handled = true, so a dispatcher exception still terminates the process. That is the right conservative default for E1, where there is no UI at all.

Once the tray icon exists (E9) the tradeoff changes and needs a real decision:
  A. Keep terminating. Honest, but a transient UI glitch in the status window kills the supervisor, which silently stops probing and unmounting. For a tool whose entire purpose is reacting to hosts going away, dying quietly is arguably the worst outcome.
  B. Set e.Handled = true, log, and show a balloon. The supervisor keeps running. Risk: the app limps along in an unknown state, which is how a mount gets left up while its host is gone — an Invariant I2 violation by a different route.
  C. Split the difference: handle exceptions originating from UI code, terminate on anything from the supervisor path.

The I2 angle is what makes this more than a style question, and it is why it should be decided deliberately rather than defaulted. Note that terminating the process is NOT automatically safe either: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §6 already requires adopt-or-clear of existing mounts on the next start, so a crash with mounts up is a handled case — but only if the user restarts Bosun.

Decide during E9, alongside the balloon-notification work.

title: needs-decision: should the fragment ship custom colour schemes? (E7)
description:
Surfaced by verified research (see bs-3ir design notes).

A fragment may declare colour schemes in a top-level "schemes" array, and scheme names resolve in ONE GLOBAL NAMESPACE merged from the user's settings.json and every installed fragment. Microsoft documents no collision or precedence behaviour for duplicate scheme names - a genuine documentation gap, not something we can look up.

docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md gives each host a `session.color_scheme` (example config uses "Campbell", a Terminal built-in) and a separate `session.tab_color`. So today Bosun only REFERENCES scheme names; it does not define any.

Options:
  A. Reference existing scheme names only; never emit a "schemes" array. Zero collision risk. The user must have the named scheme already, and validation cannot check that (we cannot read settings.json - Invariant I5).
  B. Ship one namespaced Bosun scheme (e.g. "Bosun Default") as a fallback. Small collision risk, better first-run experience.

Recommendation: A, for v1. It matches ADR-010's warning against premature generalisation, and the example config already uses a Terminal built-in. Revisit only if a real host needs a scheme that does not exist.

Note the interaction with I5: because we must never read settings.json, an invalid colour_scheme name cannot be validated and will fail silently at Terminal's end. Worth surfacing in docs/OPERATIONS.md triage regardless of which option is chosen.
close_reason: Decided per the recorded recommendation: reference existing scheme names only, never emit a schemes array. Zero collision risk in Terminal's single global scheme namespace (collision behaviour is undocumented), and shipping one later is purely additive

title: Amend ADR-006 and I5 with the verified fragment path and GUID algorithm
description:
ADR-006's implementation note asked for exactly this verification; it is now done (bs-3ir design notes) and two details in the spec need correcting.

1. PATH. ADR-006 and CLAUDE.md Invariant I5 both write the fragment location as "...\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\", omitting the "Microsoft\" segment. The verified per-user path is:
     %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Bosun\bosun.json

2. THE STORE-VS-UNPACKAGED NOTE IS A RED HERRING. ADR-006 says "The fragment directory differs between Store and unpackaged Terminal installs." Verified: it does not. Both the ProgramData and LocalAppData Fragments directories are read regardless of how Terminal itself was installed. The Store distinction applies only to Store-PACKAGED APPLICATIONS registering profiles via an app-extension manifest (PublicFolder\Fragments), a different mechanism that an unpackaged win-x64 EXE like Bosun does not use. Replace the note with the verified fact so nobody re-litigates it.

3. GUID WORDING. ADR-006 says fragments "yield stable profile GUIDs derived from source name plus profile name". Directionally right; the precise mechanism is UUIDv5 over a fixed namespace, two levels deep. Record the algorithm and the published test vector.

CLAUDE.md I5's substance (never read, write, or merge settings.json) is CORRECT and must not change - only the path text.

Caution: CLAUDE.md §2 is mirrored into the five .claude/agents/*.md definitions, which carry their own copies of the load-bearing rules. If I5's text changes, check whether the agent definitions quote the path and keep them in sync (CLAUDE.md §6 says both are reviewed artifacts).

Do this alongside E7 implementation, not before - the path should be proven by working code first.
close_reason: Superseded by E7d, which does the same amendment but sequenced after the path is proven by working code

title: CLAUDE.md §3 references `bd sync`, which does not exist in bd 1.2.2
description:
CLAUDE.md §3 says: "When you finish a unit of work, close its issue and run `bd sync` so the JSONL lands in git alongside the code." There is no `bd sync` command in the installed bd 1.1.0 — the command list has no such entry.

What actually happens now: bd 1.1.0 uses Dolt, storing issue data in .beads/embeddeddolt/, which .beads/.gitignore excludes. So issue state does NOT reach git by default and would not survive a fresh clone.

Mitigation already applied during seeding: `bd config set export.auto true` and `export.path issues.jsonl`, so .beads/issues.jsonl is written after write commands (throttled ~60s) and can be committed. This preserves the documented intent ("the JSONL export is committed, the SQLite db is not" — root .gitignore).

Decision needed from the maintainer:
1. Update CLAUDE.md §3 to say `bd export` + commit (or just 'commit .beads/issues.jsonl'), replacing the `bd sync` reference; and
2. Decide whether to also use Dolt remotes (`bd dolt push` to origin, already wired by bd init as git+https://github.com/bbuehne/bosun.git) or keep JSONL-only. Note bd init configured that remote but nothing has been pushed to it.

Also stale: root .gitignore's Beads block still mentions the SQLite db (.beads/*.db), which is the pre-Dolt layout.
notes:
UPDATE after upgrading bd 1.1.0 -> 1.2.2 (2026-08-16):

`bd sync` still does not exist, and now we know why. Per `bd info --whats-new`,
v1.2.2 is a RE-RELEASE of the tested 1.1 line (identical code to v1.1.2), issued
to supersede the accidental, untested v1.2.0/v1.2.1. The release note states
explicitly that the 1.2.x-only features -- leases, events journal, **bd sync**,
serve HTTP API, provenance -- are NOT included.

So `bd sync` existed only in a pulled, untested release. It is not a syntax drift
we can wait out, and it may never return under that name. CLAUDE.md §3 should be
corrected rather than left pending.

Also confirmed from the changelog (v1.0.5): "JSONL auto-export and auto-staging
are now opt-in - set export.auto=true and export.git-add=true to keep the old
behavior. Dolt is the canonical store." This validates enabling export.auto
during seeding. Consider also setting export.git-add=true so .beads/issues.jsonl
is staged automatically rather than remembered by hand.

Upgrade itself was clean: 15 issues, 13 edges, no cycles, no schema migration
required (our DB was created by 1.1.0 and never touched by the withdrawn v1.2.1,
which is the case that would have refused to open).
RESOLVED in CLAUDE.md §3 on 2026-08-16: the `bd sync` reference is replaced with "commit .beads/issues.jsonl", plus a note that export.auto is enabled, that `bd export` forces a refresh, and that the Dolt DB is gitignored so the commit is what makes the graph survive a clone.

title: Replace the vacuous late-fault test in the E6 suite
description:
SystemEventSupervisorAdapterTests.A_late_fault_after_the_budget_elapsed_can_be_set_without_throwing asserts that TaskCompletionSource.TrySetException does not throw - a property of TaskCompletionSource, not of the adapter. Deleting the ContinueWith block from WaitForSuspendDrainAsync entirely leaves it passing. Its own XML comment concedes the real claim is 'a direct reading of the source'.

By the project's own rule - every test must be able to fail for one describable reason - it should be replaced with something that can fail, or removed.

Also flagged, less severely: Suspend_via_the_full_synchronous_event_path_calls_SuspendAsync_and_returns_once_it_completes overclaims in its name. With no pending suspend armed, SuspendAsync returns an already-completed task, so WhenAny resolves without the budget mattering and the blocking wrapper is never actually observed to block. It proves wiring, not the synchronous path. The adversarial suite's equivalent does block and then unblock.

title: Fragment profiles have no icon and a fixed startingDirectory — no config fields exist
description:
Two profile fields E7 can emit but has nothing to populate from.

1. ICON. docs/WORK-BREAKDOWN.md E7 lists "icon" among the fields to serialise, and FragmentProfile.Icon exists, but there is no session.icon in docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md, so every profile gets Terminal's default icon. Either add session.icon to the schema or drop icon from E7's stated scope so the spec and the code agree.

Note from the bs-3ir research: on Terminal >= 1.24 a fragment may use a path relative to its own directory; on earlier versions only a web URL works for a fragment-relative icon. So shipping icon files alongside the fragment has a version floor worth knowing before designing this.

2. STARTINGDIRECTORY is fixed at %USERPROFILE% for every profile, because CONFIG-SCHEMA has no field for it. E7 sets it explicitly rather than omitting it, which is correct - Terminal's docs self-contradict on the default (they state %USERPROFILE% then list four launch-context-dependent values), so omitting it would mean depending on undocumented behaviour. But a per-host starting directory is an obvious want for a tool whose whole point is per-host workflows.

Neither blocks anything. Both are small schema additions if wanted.

title: Host keys are not validated against rclone remote-name rules
description:
RcloneRemoteNaming derives remote names as bosun-<hostKey>, but does not check that the result is a legal rclone remote name. rclone's fspath.CheckConfigName may be stricter than TOML bare-key syntax in edge cases.

Current behaviour: an illegal name surfaces as an rc-level error at mount or provisioning time rather than as an upfront config-validation error the user can locate and fix.

Low priority - it takes an unusual host key to trigger - but it is the same 'locatable error at startup beats a mysterious failure later' principle E2's validation is built on. Fold into a future config-validation pass rather than doing it standalone.

Also in the same area: global.rclone_config_path's %APPDATA% token is expanded only at the RcloneProcessService DI wiring point; ConfigParser and ConfigValidator never touch it. Worth a consistency pass so environment-variable expansion happens in exactly one place.

title: Spec cleanups: duplicate-host-key rule, none-mode drive claims, ordinal display_name
description:
Three small findings from independent adversarial testing of E2. Grouped because each is a line or two.

1. DUPLICATE HOST KEY IS UNREACHABLE AS A VALIDATION RULE. docs/CONFIG-SCHEMA.md lists it among the nine rules, but TOML forbids redefining a table, so Tomlyn rejects it at PARSE time - verified by test. E2 deliberately did not implement it rather than add dead code. Add a one-line note to the schema saying where it actually fires, so nobody later adds a ConfigValidator check looking for a condition that cannot occur.

2. DOES A mode = "none" HOST CLAIM ITS LEFTOVER DRIVE LETTER? Today it participates in collision detection, so a jump host with a commented-out mode and a stale drive = "N:" blocks the NAS from using N:. The schema says "two hosts claiming the same drive letter", and a none-mode host mounts nothing, so arguably it claims nothing. Needs a decision; the test-author deliberately wrote no test either way. (It DID test that the letter FORMAT is still validated for none-mode hosts, since that rule is stated unconditionally.)

3. DUPLICATE display_name IS COMPARED ORDINALLY, so "Prod" and "prod" coexist. Whether `wt -p` disambiguates those is unknown - Microsoft does not document tie-breaking for duplicate profile names (see bs-3ir design notes). Since E7's profile launching depends on display_name uniqueness, case-insensitive comparison is probably safer. Low priority but cheap.

None of these blocks anything.
notes:
PARTIALLY RESOLVED by the validation audit: duplicate display_name is now compared case-insensitively (item 3), and CONFIG-SCHEMA.md now records that "duplicate host key" fires at PARSE time and can never reach ConfigValidator (item 1).

STILL OPEN, item 2: does a mode = "none" host with a leftover `drive` key claim that letter? Today it participates in collision detection, so a jump host with a commented-out mode and a stale drive = "N:" blocks the NAS from using N:. Deliberately left untouched by the audit - it needs a decision, not an implementation choice.
